Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 44, verses 1–2:

Surat al-Dukhan

It is Meccan, as narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn al-Zubayr, may Allah be pleased with them, except for part of His saying, ﴿Indeed, We will remove the punishment a little; indeed, you will return [to disbelief]﴾ (Qur'an 44:15). Its number of verses, as al-Dani said, is fifty-nine according to the Kufan count, seven according to the Basran count, and six according to the count of the rest. Its points of difference, according to what is in Majma' al-Bayan, are four verses: (Ha Mim, wa-inna ha'ulaa'i la-yaqulun) is Kufan; (shajarat al-zaqqum) is Iraqi, Syrian; and the first Medinan (fi al-butun) is Iraqi, Meccan, and the last Medinan.

The connection of this surah with what precedes it is that He, Mighty and Majestic, concluded the previous surah with threat and warning, and opened this one with some severe warning. There, He, glorified be He, mentioned the saying of the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace: ﴿O my Lord, these are a people who do not believe﴾ (Qur'an 43:88). Here is its counterpart, in what He related concerning his brother Musa, peace be upon them both, in His saying, ﴿So he called upon his Lord, "These are a criminal people"﴾ (Qur'an 44:22). Also, He mentioned in what preceded, ﴿So turn away from them and say, "Peace"﴾ (Qur'an 43:89), and He, glorified be He, related about Musa, peace be upon him, ﴿And indeed, I have sought refuge in my Lord and your Lord, lest you stone me﴾ and ﴿And if you do not believe me, then leave me alone﴾ (Qur'an 44:20–21). It is close to close, and so on. It is one of the similar surahs which the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, used to recite in prayer, as al-Tabarani reported from Ibn Mas'ud: al-Dhariyat, al-Tur, al-Najm, Iqtarabat, al-Rahman, al-Waqi'ah, Nun, al-Haqqah, al-Muzzammil, La Uqsimu bi-Yawm al-Qiyamah, Hal Ata 'ala al-Insan, al-Mursalat, 'Amma Yatasa'alun, al-Nazi'at, 'Abasa, Wayl lil-Mutaffifin, Idha al-Shamsu Kuwwirat, and al-Dukhan. Reports about its virtue have also come.

Al-Tirmidhi, Muhammad ibn Nasr, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi reported from Abu Hurayrah who said: The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: "Whoever recites Ha Mim al-Dukhan in a night, seventy thousand angels will seek forgiveness for him by the morning." The same reporters also narrated from him, traced to the Prophet: "Whoever recites Ha Mim al-Dukhan on the night of Friday, will be forgiven by the morning." In a narration of al-Bayhaqi and Ibn al-Durays from him, traced to the Prophet: "Whoever recites on the night of Friday Ha Mim al-Dukhan and Ya Sin, will be forgiven by the morning." Ibn al-Durays reported from al-Hasan that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: "Whoever recites Surat al-Dukhan in a night, his past sins will be forgiven." Ibn Mardawayh reported from Abu Umamah who said: The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: "Whoever recites Ha Mim al-Dukhan on the night of Friday or the day of Friday, Allah will build for him a house in Paradise."

In the name of Allah, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 44, verse 3:

﴿Indeed, We sent it down﴾, that is, the Clear Book, which is the Qur'an, according to the most relied-upon opinion, ﴿on a blessed night﴾. It is the Night of Power (Laylat al-Qadr), as is related from Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah, Ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, Ibn Zayd and al-Hasan. Most of the exegetes hold this view, and the apparent meanings of the texts are in agreement with them. 'Ikrimah and a group (of scholars) said: it is the night of the middle of Sha'ban. It is called the Night of Mercy, the Blessed Night, the Night of the Ṣakk (the document), and the Night of al-Baraʾah (acquittal). The reason for naming it by the last two is that the bundar (the tax collector), when he had fully collected the kharaj (land tax) from its people, wrote them a baraʾah (a receipt of quittance), and likewise, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, writes for His believing servants the baraʾah and the ṣakk on this night. The apparent sense of their words here is that al-baraʾah, which is the verbal noun of baraʾa baraʾatan (meaning to be freed/cleared), is applied to a document of deeds, debts and what resembles them, and that this usage occurs in the reports; this is a well-known metaphor, and by this it has become almost like a homonym. In al-Maghrib, it says: "He was cleared of the debt or the defect (baraʾa min al-dayn wa al-ʿayb) baraʾatan," and from this comes al-baraʾah (the document) for the writ of acquittal; its plural is barāʾāt and barawāt, which is colloquial. End of quote.

Most lexicographers hold that it has not been heard from the Arabs, and that it is purely colloquial, although it falls under the broad category of metaphor.

Ibn al-Sayyid said in al-Muqtaḍab: "Al-baraʾah in origin is the verbal noun of baraʾa baraʾatan. As for al-baraʾah used in the craft of writing, its being so named is either because it is from baraʾa min dayni-hi (he was cleared of his debt) when he paid it, and baraʾtu min al-amr (I was freed from the matter) when I disengaged from it; so it is as if the one required to do something is freed from it toward the claimant, or released. It has also been said: its origin is that when a criminal committed an offence and the king pardoned him, he would write him a writ of safe-conduct from what he feared, and it was said: 'The sultan wrote to so-and-so a baraʾah.' Then this was generalised to what was written by those in authority and their like." End of quote.

They have mentioned numerous reports concerning the virtue of this night. Among them is what Ibn Majah and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman transmitted from ʿAli, may Allah honour his face, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When it is the night of the middle of Sha'ban, stand in prayer during its night and fast during its day, for Allah, the Exalted, descends in it at sunset to the lowest heaven and says: 'Is there any seeker of forgiveness, that I may forgive him? Is there any seeker of provision, that I may provide for him? Is there any afflicted one, that I may heal him? Is there such-and-such? Is there such-and-such?' until the dawn rises."

And what al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Abi Shaybah, al-Bayhaqi and Ibn Majah transmitted: from ʿAʾishah, who said: "I missed the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) one night, so I went out seeking him, and behold, he was at al-Baqi', raising his head towards the sky. He said: 'O ʿAʾishah, did you fear that Allah and His Messenger would deal unjustly with you?' I said: 'Nothing of that is in me, but I thought you had gone to one of your wives.' He said: 'Indeed Allah, Mighty and Majestic, descends on the night of the middle of Sha'ban to the lowest heaven, and forgives more than the number of the hair of the flocks of the tribe of Kalb.'"

And what Ahmad ibn Hanbal transmitted in al-Musnad from ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAs that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Allah, the Exalted, looks upon His creation on the night of the middle of Sha'ban and forgives all His servants except two: the one who harbours enmity and the murderer."

Some have mentioned a particular prayer for it, and that it equals twenty accepted pilgrimages and twenty years of accepted fasting, and they related a long hadith on this from ʿAli, may Allah honour his face. al-Bayhaqi transmitted it and then said: "This hadith is likely to be fabricated; it is munkar, and among its transmitters are unknown persons." The preachers have spoken at length about this night, its merits and its special qualities, and they mentioned a number of reports that the terms (al-ajal) are copied out in it. Al-Durr al-Manthur contains a considerable portion of this, and we shall mention some of it, Allah willing. In al-Bahr, the Hafiz Abu Bakr ibn al-ʿArabi said: "Nothing concerning it is authentic, nor is the copying out of the terms in it; and this is not free from rash assertion. And Allah knows best."

The meaning of His sending it down in that night is that it was sent down in it all at once to the lowest heaven from the Preserved Tablet. The sending down in parts over twenty-three years or less was from the lowest heaven. This has been related from Ibn Jarir and others, and he mentioned that the place in that heaven where it was sent down is the House Frequented (al-Bayt al-Ma'mur), which is directly opposite the Ka'bah, such that if it had fallen, it would have fallen upon it.

Sa'id ibn Mansur transmitted from Ibrahim al-Nakha'i that he said: "The Qur'an was sent down entirely to Jibril, peace be upon him, and Jibril, peace be upon him, would later bring it to the Prophet (ﷺ)."

Others have said: the meaning is that its sending down began in that night, by a figurative usage in the time-frame or in the attribution. This was objected to on the grounds that the beginning of the year is Muharram or Rabi' al-Awwal, because he (ﷺ) was born in it, and from it the calendar was reckoned during his lifetime until the caliphate of ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, and this is the most correct view. Moreover, revelation came to him (ﷺ) at the age of forty, according to the well-known view among several opinions. So how can the beginning of the sending down be in the Night of Power in the month of Ramadan, or in the Night of Acquittal in Sha'ban?

It was answered that the beginning of revelation was a dream in the month of Rabi' al-Awwal, and it was not with the sending down of any part of the Qur'an; and revelation in wakefulness together with the sending down was on Monday, seventeen days past the month of Ramadan. It was also said: seven days into it; and it was said: twenty-four nights into it. You know the great divergence of opinions in this matter, so whoever holds that the sending down began in a month will be bound by what does not contradict it.

There has been disagreement about the first thing that was sent down of it. In Sahih Muslim it is ﴿O you wrapped in garments﴾ (al-Muddaththir). al-Nawawi criticised this in his commentary, saying: "It is weak, rather false; the correct view is that the first thing sent down, absolutely, was ﴿Read in the name of your Lord﴾ (al-ʿAlaq), as stated in the hadith of ʿAʾishah. As for ﴿O you wrapped in garments﴾, its sending down was after the interruption of revelation, as stated in the transmission of al-Zuhri from Abu Salamah, from Jabir."

As for the saying of those exegetes who claim the first thing sent down was al-Fatihah, its falsity is too evident to mention. The discussion of this is complete in al-Itqan, so whoever wishes should refer to it. End of quote.

The description of the night as blessed is because the sending down of the Qur'an entails all the religious and worldly benefits together; or because in it there is the descent of the angels, mercy, the answering of supplication and the excellence of worship; or because in it there is the determining of provisions, the distinguishing of decrees such as the terms and others, and the granting of the complete intercession to him (ﷺ). This is on the basis that it is the Night of Acquittal, for it has been related that the Prophet (ﷺ) asked on the thirteenth night of Sha'ban for his community, and was given a third of them; then he asked on the fourteenth night and was given two-thirds; then he asked on the fifteenth night and was given all of them, except those who ran away from Allah like a runaway camel.

Whatever the case, it has been said that the explanation is only needed on the basis of the view chosen by al-ʿIzz ibn ʿAbd al-Salam, that places and times are all equal in themselves, and none is superior to another except by what occurs in them of deeds and the like. Some added: or that the place which contained him (ﷺ) should be entered, for it is the best of the earthly and heavenly places, to the extent that it has been said: "And I say by it, it is better than the Throne."

The truth is that it is not far-fetched that Allah, glorified is He, singles out some of it with a special honour, so that this becomes a motive for the responsible person to undertake deeds in it, or for another wisdom.

The clause ﴿Indeed, We sent it down﴾ is the answer to the oath, and in this there is emphasis, like what is in the verse:

"And your front teeth, indeed they are 'Ighriḍ (bright, pure)."

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, We have always been warners﴾ is a resumptive clause explaining the reason for the sending down,

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 44, verse 4–5:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Therein every wise matter is made distinct﴾ is also a resumptive clause (isti'naf) to explain the specification of the blessed night. It is as if it were said: We sent it down because it is part of Our way to warn and to caution against punishment, and its sending down in that blessed night was because it is among the matters that indicate far-reaching wisdoms, and it is a night in which every wise matter is made distinct. So in the speech there is laff wa nashr (a arrangement of elements in a combined and then separated manner). The stipulation that each of the two be in two independent clauses is something for which there is no need. It was also said: the clause ﴿Therein is made distinct﴾ etc. is another attribute of the night, and what lies between them is a parenthetical insertion (i'tiraD) that does not harm the separation caused by it; rather, separation by it is not considered a separation. It was also said that His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed We were ever warners﴾ is the answer to the oath, and what lies between them is a parenthetical insertion. This is the view of Ibn 'Atiyya, who claimed that it is not permissible to make ﴿Indeed We sent it down﴾ its answer, because of what it contains of swearing by a thing upon itself.

It has been objected that His saying, ﴿Therein every wise matter is made distinct﴾, would then be a continuation of the parenthetical insertion, so it would not be good for it to be delayed after the thing sworn to. It is not resolved by saying that this clause is a resumptive clause and not another attribute, because it is an explanatory resumption (isti'naf bayani) connected with what precedes it, as you have heard just now; so separation is also unfitting, as is not hidden from one who has sound taste. As for what was mentioned about swearing by a thing upon itself, we have already pointed to its answer. It was also said that His saying, glorified is He, ﴿Indeed We were ever warners﴾ is another answer to the oath, and in that there is a plurality of the thing sworn to without conjunction; we have not seen anyone address this.

The meaning of yufraqu is "is detailed and summarised." Al-hakim here means al-muhkam (the firmly decreed), because it is not changed or altered after it is presented to the angels, peace be upon them, unlike before that, when it is in the Preserved Tablet, for Allah, exalted is He, erases from it what He wills and confirms.

It is also permissible that it means "that which is judged with" (al-mahkum bihi), and its attribution to the matter is then literal. It is also permissible that the meaning is "every matter connected with wisdom," the original being "its possessor is wise," so the attribution was used figuratively. It was also said: hakim is for attribution, like tamir and laban (having dates, having milk), and He, glorified is He, has left this matter vague.

Muhammad ibn Nasr, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas that he said concerning this: "There is written from Umm al-Kitab on the Night of Power what will occur during the year of provision, death, life or rain, until it is written: the pilgrim will perform Hajj, so-and-so will perform Hajj, and so-and-so will perform Hajj."

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir related from Rabi'a ibn Kulthum who said: "I was with al-Hasan, when a man said to him: 'O Abu Sa'id, is the Night of Power in every Ramadan?' He said: 'Yes, by Allah, it is indeed in every Ramadan, and it is a night in which every wise matter is made distinct: therein Allah, exalted is He, decrees every term, deed and provision until its like.'" This generalisation has been related from more than one of the early Muslims.

Al-Bayhaqi related from Abu al-Jawza' concerning ﴿Therein every wise matter is made distinct﴾: "It is the Night of Power. The Greatest Register is brought, year after year, and Allah, exalted is His majesty, forgives whom He wills. Do you not see that He, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿A mercy from your Lord﴾?" There is a point of discussion in this. To this same generalisation went some of those who said that the blessed night is the Night of Acquittal (laylat al-bara'a). Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related through Muhammad ibn Suqa from 'Ikrima that he said concerning the verse: "On the night of the middle of Sha'ban the affair of the year is firmly settled, the living are separated from the dead, and the pilgrim is registered; not one of them is added to or subtracted from." In many reports, the limitation is only to the determining of terms. Ibn Jarir and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman related from al-Zuhri, from 'Uthman ibn Muhammad ibn al-Mughira ibn al-Akhfash who said: (The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: "Terms are cut off from Sha'ban to Sha'ban, so much so that a man marries and has children, and yet his name has already come out among the dead.") Al-Dinawari related in al-Mujalasa from Rashid ibn Sa'd that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: ("On the night of the middle of Sha'ban, Allah, exalted is He, reveals to the Angel of Death to seize every soul he intends to seize in that year.") Similar reports are many. It has also been said: they begin copying every wise matter from the Preserved Tablet on the Night of Acquittal, and the completion occurs on the Night of Power. The register of provisions is handed to Mika'il, peace be upon him; the register of wars to Jibril, peace be upon him; likewise earthquakes, thunderbolts and sinking of the earth; and the register of deeds to Isma'il, peace be upon him, lord of the lowest heaven, who is a mighty angel; and the register of calamities to the Angel of Death.

It is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that all decrees are decided on the night of the middle of Sha'ban and delivered to their holders on the night of the twenty-seventh of Ramadan. Objection has been raised to the use of apparent meanings to establish that the mentioned night is the Night of Power and not the night of the middle of Sha'ban, but whoever reflects will know that it does not damage the apparent meanings. Yes, it is related from 'Ikrima that the night of the middle of Sha'ban is the Night of Power, and this requires interpreting what its apparent meaning refuses; so reflect. The discussion of this point will come, Allah willing, exalted is He, in full and in the best manner in the commentary on Surat al-Qadr, and He, glorified is He, is the Granter of success.

al-Hasan, al-A'raj and al-A'mash read (yafruqu) with a fatha on the ya' and a damma on the ra', (kulla) in the accusative, meaning "Allah, exalted is He, makes distinct." Zayd ibn 'Ali, as reported by al-Zamakhshari from him, read (nafruqu) with a nun, (kulla) in the accusative; and as reported by Abu 'Ali al-Ahwazi from him, with a fatha on the ya' and a kasra on the ra', (kalla) in the accusative, and (hakimun) in the nominative as the subject of yafriqu. Al-Hasan and Za'ida from al-A'mash read (yufarraqu) with shadda and the passive form, and it is for intensification. In this there is a refutation of the view of some lexicographers such as al-Hariri that al-farq (separation) is specific to meanings and al-tafriq (dispersal) to physical bodies.

﴿A matter from Us﴾ is put in the accusative by specification (ikhtisas), and its indefiniteness is for magnification. The prepositional phrase is in the position of an attribute to it, and attaching it to yufraqu is nothing. The intended meaning of "from Us" is that it is in accordance with wisdom and planning, i.e., "I mean by this matter a magnificent matter, arising according to the requirement of Our wisdom and planning." It is an explanation of its increased grandeur and praise. It is also permissible that it be a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun of the preceding matter hidden in hakim, which is an attribute of it, or from (amr) itself. The coming of the circumstantial clause from it is valid even though it is indefinite, because it is specified by the description. Moreover, the generality of the indefinite noun that is annexed is enough to justify the circumstantial sense without the need for a description. The saying of al-Samin that in this there is the view of a circumstantial clause from the annexed-to noun in cases other than those mentioned in grammar comes from a weak consideration, because it is like a part in permissibility of dispensing with it, such that one says: "yufraqu amrun hakimun," intending the generality of the indefinite in affirmation, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿A soul knows what it has presented﴾. It has also been said that it is a circumstantial clause from (kull). In any case it is different from the one it qualifies, because it is described by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿from Us﴾, so its occurrence as a circumstantial clause is valid without linguistic defect in it.

That it be emphatic is not possible together with being a description, as is not hidden from one of sound mind. On these aspects it is one of the matters. It is also permissible that by it be meant the matter which is the opposite of prohibition, so that it is one of the commands; in that case it is in the accusative as an infinitive (masdar) of a verb implied from its own root, i.e., "We have commanded a command from Us," and the sentence is an explanation of His saying, glorified is He: ﴿is made distinct﴾, etc. It has been said: either it is in the accusative as an infinitive for yufraqu, because Allah's decreeing of a thing is its obligation, and likewise His command concerning it, as if it were said: "Every matter sought in accordance with wisdom is commanded as a command," so amr is placed in the position of furqan (distinction), which is used in the sense of command. Or it is in the circumstantial sense from the subject of (anzalna) or its object, i.e., "We sent it down commanding a command," or while the Book is "a command that must be carried out." In making the Book itself the command, because it contains it, there is also a figurative sense in it, conveying magnificence. This was criticised in al-Kashf, which said: "In it there is weakness, because of the separation by the two clauses between the circumstantial clause and its owner according to the second, and because the commands issued by Him are not specific to that night according to the first."

Its aspect is that it be specified to the Qur'an, and that His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Therein is made distinct﴾ not be made a cause of the sending down on the night; rather it is a detailing of what was summarised in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Indeed We sent it down on a blessed night﴾, in the sense that: "Therein was sent down the Clear Book, which comprises every commanded wise matter," as if He made the whole Book a command, or what He commanded comprises all commanded things. In this there is a fine exaggeration. It is not hidden that understanding this from the verse involves strain.

Al-Khafaji said concerning the matter of separation: that separation does not harm the parenthetical insertion, and likewise the causal reading, because it is not alien.

Some permitted, on the assumption that the command is meant as the opposite of prohibition, that it is an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu), and its governing element is ﴿is made distinct﴾, or "We sent down", or ﴿warners﴾.

Zayd ibn 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with both of them, read (amrun) in the nominative, and this supports that its accusative in the reading of the majority is by specification, since the nominative is upon it in that reading. And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed We were ever sending messengers﴾

It was also said: the clause ﴿Therein is made distinct﴾ etc. is another attribute of the night, and what lies between them is a parenthetical insertion (i'tiraD) that does not harm the separation caused by it; rather, separation by it is not considered a separation. It was also said that His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed We were ever warners﴾ is the answer to the oath, and what lies between them is a parenthetical insertion. This is the view of Ibn 'Atiyya, who claimed that it is not permissible to make ﴿Indeed We sent it down﴾ its answer, because of what it contains of swearing by a thing upon itself.

It has been objected that His saying, ﴿Therein every wise matter is made distinct﴾, would then be a continuation of the parenthetical insertion, so it would not be good for it to be delayed after the thing sworn to. It is not resolved by saying that this clause is a resumptive clause and not another attribute, because it is an explanatory resumption (isti'naf bayani) connected with what precedes it, as you have heard just now; so separation is also unfitting, as is not hidden from one who has sound taste. As for what was mentioned about swearing by a thing upon itself, we have already pointed to its answer. It was also said that His saying, glorified is He, ﴿Indeed We were ever warners﴾ is another answer to the oath, and in that there is a plurality of the thing sworn to without conjunction; we have not seen anyone address this.

The meaning of yufraqu is "is detailed and summarised." Al-hakim here means al-muhkam (the firmly decreed), because it is not changed or altered after it is presented to the angels, peace be upon them, unlike before that, when it is in the Preserved Tablet, for Allah, exalted is He, erases from it what He wills and confirms.

It is also permissible that it means "that which is judged with" (al-mahkum bihi), and its attribution to the matter is then literal. It is also permissible that the meaning is "every matter connected with wisdom," the original being "its possessor is wise," so the attribution was used figuratively. It was also said: hakim is for attribution, like tamir and laban (having dates, having milk), and He, glorified is He, has left this matter vague.

Muhammad ibn Nasr, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas that he said concerning this: "There is written from Umm al-Kitab on the Night of Power what will occur during the year of provision, death, life or rain, until it is written: the pilgrim will perform Hajj, so-and-so will perform Hajj, and so-and-so will perform Hajj."

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir related from Rabi'a ibn Kulthum who said: "I was with al-Hasan, when a man said to him: 'O Abu Sa'id, is the Night of Power in every Ramadan?' He said: 'Yes, by Allah, it is indeed in every Ramadan, and it is a night in which every wise matter is made distinct: therein Allah, exalted is He, decrees every term, deed and provision until its like.'" This generalisation has been related from more than one of the early Muslims.

Al-Bayhaqi related from Abu al-Jawza' concerning ﴿Therein every wise matter is made distinct﴾: "It is the Night of Power. The Greatest Register is brought, year after year, and Allah, exalted is His majesty, forgives whom He wills. Do you not see that He, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿A mercy from your Lord﴾?" There is a point of discussion in this. To this same generalisation went some of those who said that the blessed night is the Night of Acquittal (laylat al-bara'a). Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related through Muhammad ibn Suqa from 'Ikrima that he said concerning the verse: "On the night of the middle of Sha'ban the affair of the year is firmly settled, the living are separated from the dead, and the pilgrim is registered; not one of them is added to or subtracted from." In many reports, the limitation is only to the determining of terms. Ibn Jarir and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman related from al-Zuhri, from 'Uthman ibn Muhammad ibn al-Mughira ibn al-Akhfash who said: (The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: "Terms are cut off from Sha'ban to Sha'ban, so much so that a man marries and has children, and yet his name has already come out among the dead.") Al-Dinawari related in al-Mujalasa from Rashid ibn Sa'd that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: ("On the night of the middle of Sha'ban, Allah, exalted is He, reveals to the Angel of Death to seize every soul he intends to seize in that year.") Similar reports are many. It has also been said: they begin copying every wise matter from the Preserved Tablet on the Night of Acquittal, and the completion occurs on the Night of Power. The register of provisions is handed to Mika'il, peace be upon him; the register of wars to Jibril, peace be upon him; likewise earthquakes, thunderbolts and sinking of the earth; and the register of deeds to Isma'il, peace be upon him, lord of the lowest heaven, who is a mighty angel; and the register of calamities to the Angel of Death.

It is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that all decrees are decided on the night of the middle of Sha'ban and delivered to their holders on the night of the twenty-seventh of Ramadan. Objection has been raised to the use of apparent meanings to establish that the mentioned night is the Night of Power and not the night of the middle of Sha'ban, but whoever reflects will know that it does not damage the apparent meanings. Yes, it is related from 'Ikrima that the night of the middle of Sha'ban is the Night of Power, and this requires interpreting what its apparent meaning refuses; so reflect. The discussion of this point will come, Allah willing, exalted is He, in full and in the best manner in the commentary on Surat al-Qadr, and He, glorified is He, is the Granter of success.

al-Hasan, al-A'raj and al-A'mash read (yafruqu) with a fatha on the ya' and a damma on the ra', (kulla) in the accusative, meaning "Allah, exalted is He, makes distinct." Zayd ibn 'Ali, as reported by al-Zamakhshari from him, read (nafruqu) with a nun, (kulla) in the accusative; and as reported by Abu 'Ali al-Ahwazi from him, with a fatha on the ya' and a kasra on the ra', (kalla) in the accusative, and (hakimun) in the nominative as the subject of yafriqu. Al-Hasan and Za'ida from al-A'mash read (yufarraqu) with shadda and the passive form, and it is for intensification. In this there is a refutation of the view of some lexicographers such as al-Hariri that al-farq (separation) is specific to meanings and al-tafriq (dispersal) to physical bodies.

﴿A matter from Us﴾ is put in the accusative by specification (ikhtisas), and its indefiniteness is for magnification. The prepositional phrase is in the position of an attribute to it, and attaching it to yufraqu is nothing. The intended meaning of "from Us" is that it is in accordance with wisdom and planning, i.e., "I mean by this matter a magnificent matter, arising according to the requirement of Our wisdom and planning." It is an explanation of its increased grandeur and praise. It is also permissible that it be a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun of the preceding matter hidden in hakim, which is an attribute of it, or from (amr) itself. The coming of the circumstantial clause from it is valid even though it is indefinite, because it is specified by the description. Moreover, the generality of the indefinite noun that is annexed is enough to justify the circumstantial sense without the need for a description. The saying of al-Samin that in this there is the view of a circumstantial clause from the annexed-to noun in cases other than those mentioned in grammar comes from a weak consideration, because it is like a part in permissibility of dispensing with it, such that one says: "yufraqu amrun hakimun," intending the generality of the indefinite in affirmation, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿A soul knows what it has presented﴾. It has also been said that it is a circumstantial clause from (kull). In any case it is different from the one it qualifies, because it is described by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿from Us﴾, so its occurrence as a circumstantial clause is valid without linguistic defect in it.

That it be emphatic is not possible together with being a description, as is not hidden from one of sound mind. On these aspects it is one of the matters. It is also permissible that by it be meant the matter which is the opposite of prohibition, so that it is one of the commands; in that case it is in the accusative as an infinitive (masdar) of a verb implied from its own root, i.e., "We have commanded a command from Us," and the sentence is an explanation of His saying, glorified is He: ﴿is made distinct﴾, etc. It has been said: either it is in the accusative as an infinitive for yufraqu, because Allah's decreeing of a thing is its obligation, and likewise His command concerning it, as if it were said: "Every matter sought in accordance with wisdom is commanded as a command," so amr is placed in the position of furqan (distinction), which is used in the sense of command. Or it is in the circumstantial sense from the subject of (anzalna) or its object, i.e., "We sent it down commanding a command," or while the Book is "a command that must be carried out." In making the Book itself the command, because it contains it, there is also a figurative sense in it, conveying magnificence. This was criticised in al-Kashf, which said: "In it there is weakness, because of the separation by the two clauses between the circumstantial clause and its owner according to the second, and because the commands issued by Him are not specific to that night according to the first."

Its aspect is that it be specified to the Qur'an, and that His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Therein is made distinct﴾ not be made a cause of the sending down on the night; rather it is a detailing of what was summarised in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Indeed We sent it down on a blessed night﴾, in the sense that: "Therein was sent down the Clear Book, which comprises every commanded wise matter," as if He made the whole Book a command, or what He commanded comprises all commanded things. In this there is a fine exaggeration. It is not hidden that understanding this from the verse involves strain.

Al-Khafaji said concerning the matter of separation: that separation does not harm the parenthetical insertion, and likewise the causal reading, because it is not alien.

Some permitted, on the assumption that the command is meant as the opposite of prohibition, that it is an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu), and its governing element is ﴿is made distinct﴾, or "We sent down", or ﴿warners﴾.

Zayd ibn 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with both of them, read (amrun) in the nominative, and this supports that its accusative in the reading of the majority is by specification, since the nominative is upon it in that reading. And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed We were ever sending messengers﴾

﴿A mercy from your Lord﴾ is a causal clause (ta'lil) either for ﴿is made distinct﴾ (yufraq) or for His words, exalted is He, ﴿a command from Us﴾. ﴿Mercy﴾ (rahmatan) is the direct object (maf'ul bihi) of ﴿sending﴾ (mursilin). Its tanwin (nunation) is for magnification (tafkhim), and the prepositional phrase ﴿from your Lord﴾ is in the position of an adjective describing it. The attribution of sending to mercy here is like its attribution to it in His words, glory be to Him: ﴿Whatever mercy Allah opens for the people, none can withhold it; and whatever He withholds, none can release after Him﴾. The meaning, according to what is in al-Kashshaf, is: every matter is made distinct on this night, because it is Our custom to send Our mercy, and the separating of every matter, including the distribution of provisions and other things, belongs to the category of mercy. That is, the primary and essential purpose of that is mercy.
[Page 115]
Or, the commands are issued from Us, because it is Our custom to do so. The commands issued from His direction, exalted is He, also belong to the category of mercy, because the purpose of imposing obligations on the servants is to expose them to benefits. In this there is, as it has been said, an indication that making it a causal clause for His words, glory be to Him, ﴿a command from Us﴾ is only on the assumption that by "command" is meant the opposite of prohibition (nahy), and this applies under both the assumption that it is a verbal noun (masdar) and the assumption that it is a circumstantial state (hal).

In al-Kashf it is stated that His words "it is made distinct" etc., or "the commands are issued" etc., are an explanation of the meaning of the causal clause according to the two interpretations of ﴿is made distinct﴾ (yufraq). This is because it means either separation in its literal sense, through the distribution of provisions and other things, or the meaning "is commanded," and the required matter must necessarily be something commanded. Its essence therefore returns to His words: "or the commands are issued from Us." It does not refer to the two aspects of causation regarding its connection to ﴿is made distinct﴾ or to ﴿a command﴾, since its connection to ﴿a command﴾ is valid only if it is put in the accusative by specification (ikhtisas). In that case, "command" does not mean the opposite of prohibition, because if "command" is the opposite of prohibition, it is either a verbal noun, which would then explain the causation of its own act, or a confirmatory state, which would then return to the causation of the specific sending down, and that is not the intended meaning. The meaning was not mentioned under the assumption that it is connected to ﴿a command﴾ because the first meaning is also suitable as its explanation. End of quotation.

The apparent view is that this is an explanation of the two aspects of causation. What has been said in denying this is not free from scrutiny, as becomes clear upon reflection. Taking custom into account in explaining the meaning has come from our saying "he used to do such-and-such" (kana yaf'alu kadha), for something that has repeatedly occurred and become a habit, as the scholars of hadith and others have stated in their books. To convey this, He deviated from the shorter ﴿Indeed We are senders﴾. His words, glory be to Him, ﴿from your Lord﴾, place the apparent noun in the position of the pronoun, and the original would have been ﴿from Us﴾. So the word "Lord" was used, joined to the pronoun of the Prophet (ﷺ), in order to specify the address to him (ﷺ), as an honour to him (ﷺ), and as an indication that His being your Lord, while you are sent as a mercy to the worlds, is among the things that require Him to send mercy.

Al-Tibi said: He specified the address to His Messenger (ﷺ), while the intended meaning is general. The original would have been ﴿from your Lord﴾ (addressed in the plural), and the word "Lord" was used to indicate that lordship (rububiyyah) requires mercy upon those who are lordly cared for (marbubin), and to serve as a preparation upon which the following causal clause is built, which contains an implicit allusion through restriction (hasr) that their gods do not hear, do not see, and do not avail anything. It was objected that if the generality were intended, this point would be lost, and it would follow that the believers enter into His words, exalted is He, ﴿if you are certain﴾ and what follows, and that is not the meaning. Some have said that ﴿the mercy sent﴾ refers to our Prophet (ﷺ), but it is not hidden that the soundness of the causal clause rejects this.

It is permissible that His words, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed We are ever sending﴾ be a substitute (badal) for His words, glory be to Him, ﴿Indeed We are ever warning﴾, which occurs as a causal clause for the sending down of the Book, either as a substitute of the whole (badal kull) or as a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal), in terms of sending and warning. In that case ﴿mercy﴾ would be an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu), meaning: We sent down the Qur'an, because it is Our custom to send messengers and books to the servants for the sake of mercy upon them. The choice of making mercy an object of purpose is so that the substitute and the substituted correspond, since the meaning of the substituted is "doers of warning," and "doers of sending" corresponds to it. He did not permit it to be so as a causal clause, but rather required it to be an object (maf'ul bihi), so that it would be valid, because if it were said: "In it is made distinct every decreed matter, because We are doers of sending for the sake of mercy," it would not convey that the separation is mercy, nor that He, exalted is He, is the sender, and thus the causation would not hold. It has been said that the reading of al-Hasan and Zayd ibn Ali with the nominative ﴿mercy﴾ supports the accusative reading as an object, because the sentence according to it is a resumed sentence (jumlah mustanifah), meaning: it is ﴿mercy﴾ as a causal clause for the sending, which agrees with the statement that in the accusative reading it is an object of purpose, and so their two readings agree in the meaning of ﴿Indeed We are ever sending﴾ as ﴿Indeed We are doers of sending﴾.

One of the eminent verifiers said: The view that it is a causal clause is more apparent than the view that it is a substitute, so that the discourse is in a coherent sequence following the causation, and because of what was mentioned about the situation that calls for substitution, and because of the occurrence of separation. He indicated, according to what has been said, by what was mentioned about the situation that calls for substitution, that the substituted is not intended and is in the status of being dropped, and here it is not so. This was objected to on the grounds that this is a general tendency, not an invariable rule. His words "because of the occurrence of separation," meaning between the substitute and the substituted, [are explained as follows:] the intervening element is not foreign, so the separation by it does no harm. Reflect on this.

It is also permissible that ﴿mercy﴾ be a verbal noun for an implied verb "We have shown mercy," that it be a circumstantial state from the pronoun in ﴿senders﴾, and that it be a substitute for ﴿a command﴾. So do not be heedless.

﴿Indeed He is the All-Hearing﴾ of every thing heard, so He hears the words of the servants, ﴿the All-Knowing﴾ of every thing known, so He knows their conditions. The insertion of the pronoun together with the definiteness of both terms serves to convey restriction (hasr). The clause is a confirmation of His lordship, mighty and majestic is He, and that lordship is not due except to one who has these attributes. In the specification of ﴿the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾, according to what al-Tibi said, there is an incidental inclusion (idmaj) of a warning to the disbelievers and a promise to the believers who received the mercy with various kinds of gratitude.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 44, verse 7:

﴿Lord of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them﴾ is either a substitute (badal) for ﴿your Lord﴾, or an explanatory apposition (bayan), or a qualifier (na't).

Several of the seven canonical readers, along with al-A'raj, Ibn Abi Ishaq, Abu Ja'far and Shaybah, read it in the nominative (bil-raf'), on the basis that it is a second predicate (khabar) of inna, or the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: "He is the Lord." The sentence is then resumed (mustanafah) to establish what preceded it and to give its reason: ﴿if you are certain﴾, i.e. if you are among those who possess some measure of certainty (iqan) and a portion of the certain knowledge (al-'ulum al-yaqiniyyah). This is on the understanding that the transitive descriptor is treated as intransitive (munazzal manzilat al-lazim), since there is no intention to specify its object. The apodosis (jawab al-shart) is omitted, i.e. if you are among the people of certainty, you know that He, glory be to Him, is the Lord of the heavens and the earth, since this is among the most evident of certain matters in terms of proof; and then it necessarily follows for you to say what it requires of what was mentioned earlier. It is also permissible that its object be understood, i.e. if you are certain in your affirmation when you are asked who created the heavens and the earth and you say, "Allah, exalted is He, created them." The apodosis is again omitted, i.e. if you are certain in your affirmation of that, you know what it requires of what has preceded, because its implication is evident.

Many have made the apodosis, on both readings, to be: "what we have said has been established for you." They did not permit making the content of the apodosis ﴿Lord of the heavens﴾ etc., because He, glory be to Him, is so regardless of whether they were certain or not, so there is no sense in making it indicative of that. Likewise, making it the content of what follows ("Nay, but they are in doubt") is not fitting even in terms of knowledge.

In this condition there is a treatment of their certainty as though it were absent, because its opposite is manifest against them. This is what is meant by those who said: it is of the type of treating the one who knows as the one who is ignorant, because he does not act according to the requirement of knowledge. It was said: it cannot be said that they were treated as doubters, given His words that follow, ﴿Nay, but they are in doubt﴾. I see no harm in saying that they were first treated as such, and then were recorded as being in doubt, because although they acknowledged that He, mighty and majestic, is the Lord of the heavens and the earth, they did not cease to be in doubt, due to their heresy regarding His attributes and their associating others with Him, exalted is His state.

It is also permissible that ﴿certain﴾ be a metaphor for ﴿desiring certainty﴾, with the apodosis again omitted, i.e. if you desire certainty, then know that. But this is far-fetched. As for taking ﴿in﴾ as a negation, as al-Nisaburi related, it is nothing, as is not hidden.

﴿There is no deity except Him﴾ is a resumptive sentence (jumlah musta'nafah) that confirms what precedes it. It has also been said that it is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: He, glory be to Him, is the one; there is no deity except Him. The subject and predicate together form a resumptive sentence confirming this. It has also been said that it is another predicate of "inna" according to the reading ﴿Lord of the heavens﴾ in the nominative, making it a predicate. It has also been said that it is a predicate of that (noun) according to that reading, with what lies between them being a parenthetical clause (i'tiraD). ﴿He gives life and causes death﴾ is a resumptive sentence, as is what precedes it. Likewise is the Most High's statement ﴿your Lord and the Lord of your forefathers of old﴾, read with an omitted subject, or as a substitute (badal) for "Lord of the heavens" according to that reading, or as an explanatory apposition (bayan), or as a qualifier (na't) of it. It has also been said that it is the subject of "yumit" (causes death), and in "yuhyi" (gives life) there is a pronoun referring back to it, and the sentence falls under the category of dispute over government (tanazu'), or refers back to ﴿Lord of the heavens﴾. It has also been said that ﴿He gives life and causes death﴾ is another predicate of "Rabb al-samawat", and likewise ﴿your Lord﴾. It has also been said that they are two further predicates of "inna". Ibn Abi Ishaq, Ibn Muhaysin, Abu Haywah, al-Za'faranani, Ibn Muqsim, al-Hasan, Abu Musa, 'Isa ibn Sulayman, and Salih read it in the genitive (bi'l-jarr) as a substitute for ﴿Lord of the heavens﴾, according to the genitive reading; both Kisa'i transmitters ('an al-Kisa'i) report this. Ahmad ibn Jubayr al-Antaki read it in the accusative (bi'l-nasb) as an expression of praise (al-madh).

[p. 117]

﴿Nay, they are in doubt﴾: an *idrab ibtali* (a transitional turn that nullifies what precedes it), by which their certainty is negated, since they do not act in accordance with what it requires. The tanwin on "*shakk*" (doubt) is for magnification, meaning: in a great doubt. ﴿Playing﴾: they do not say what they say in a manner that conforms to denying the matter in earnest and with conviction; rather, they say it mixed with mockery and play. This clause is a predicate following another predicate concerning them.

It is also permitted that this clause itself be the predicate, with the adverbial phrase being connected to the verb and placed first for the sake of the *fasila* (verse-ending rhyme). The shift away from addressing them directly is due to their extreme obstinacy and their failure to pay heed.

**[Page 118]**

The *fa'* in His words, ﴿So watch﴾ (*fa-irtaqib*), indicates that the watching, or the command to watch, follows from what precedes it. Their being in doubt and playing is what necessitates this decisively. That is, "Wait for them on the day when the sky brings a clear smoke." That is, on the day when it brings barrenness and famine, for the person who is extremely hungry sees between himself and the sky something like smoke. It is a darkness that appears before the eye because of its weakness, so he imagines it. The application of the word *dukhan* (smoke) to that seen thing is based on the fact that the one who sees it imagines it to be smoke. Describing it as *mubin* (clear) does not preclude this. The intended meaning of barrenness and famine is a figurative usage, of the type of mentioning the effect while intending the cause. Alternatively, the air becomes murky in a year of drought due to a great deal of dust, because of the scarcity of rain that would settle it. So it is a metonymy for drought. Abu 'Ubayda interpreted *dukhan* as this. Al-Qutabi said: it is called *dukhan* because the land dries out until something like smoke rises from it. Some Arabs said: we call the overpowering evil *dukhan*. The reason for this is that smoke is something that causes harm, so it is applied to every harmful thing resembling it. Here, drought is intended by it. Its literal meaning is well known. The analogical plural of it in the paucity form is *adkhina*, and in the abundance form is *dikhnan*, like *ghurab* (crow) with *aghriba* and *ghirban*. They took an irregular path in its plural on the pattern *fawa'il*, saying *dawakhin*, as if it were the plural of *dakhina*, notionally. The indication of figurative usage in it here is contextual, as you will know, God willing, from the report. The intended meaning of "day" is absolute time. It is either an object of *irtaqib* or an adverb for it, with the object omitted: that is, watch for the promise of God Most High on that day. By "the sky" is meant the direction of height. Attributing the bringing of that to both of them is attribution to the cause, since it occurs by their not sending rain. The attribution was not made to Him, glorified and exalted, although He is the actual agent, so that the speech with its preceding context, which includes attributing what is mercy to Him, exalted is His station, would be in the same pattern as His words, ﴿on whom You have bestowed favour, not of those who have earned anger﴾.

The interpretation of the smoke as explained above is narrated from Qatada, Abu al-'Aliya, al-Nakha'i, al-Dahhak, Mujahid and Muqatil, and it is the choice of al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj.

It has been narrated by many chains from Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him. Ahmad, al-Bukhari and a group recorded from Masruq, who said: "A man came to 'Abd Allah and said: I left a man in the mosque who says, concerning this verse, ﴿the day the sky brings a smoke﴾ etc., that smoke will overtake people before the Day of Resurrection, seizing the ears and eyes of the hypocrites, while it will affect the believer like the condition of a cold. He became angry, and he was reclining, so he sat up and said: Whoever among you has knowledge, let him speak of it, and whoever does not know, let him say: Allah knows best. For it is part of knowledge to say of what one does not know: Allah knows best. I will tell you about the smoke: when Quraysh became difficult for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and were slow to accept Islam, he said: O Allah, help me against them with seven [years] like the seven [years] of Joseph. So a drought and hardship struck them until they ate bones. A man would look at the sky and see between himself and it something like smoke, from hunger. So Allah Most High sent down: ﴿So watch for [the day] of painful [punishment]﴾. Then the Prophet (ﷺ) came, and it was said to him: O Messenger of Allah, ask Allah for rain for Mudar. So he prayed for rain for them, peace be upon him, and they were given rain. Then Allah Most High sent down: ﴿Indeed, We will remove the punishment a little; indeed, you will return﴾," the report being lengthy.

In another authentic narration, he said: "When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) saw people turning away, he said: O Allah, [send] seven [years] like the seven [years] of Joseph. So a year of drought seized them until they ate carrion, hides and bones. Then Abu Sufyan and some people of Makkah came to him and said: O Muhammad, you claim that you have been sent as a mercy, and that your people have perished. So invoke Allah. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) invoked, and they were given rain, but it continued over them for seven days. The people complained of the abundance of rain, so he said: O Allah, [let it fall] around us and not upon us. So the cloud parted from above his head, and the people were given water around them." He said: "So the sign of the smoke has passed, and it is the hunger that struck them," the hadith.

Its apparent meaning indicates, as in Ibn Kathir's *Tarikh*, that the incident took place in Makkah, so the verse is Meccan.

In some narrations, the story of Abu Sufyan was after the Hijrah, so perhaps it happened twice. What relates to this has already been mentioned in the commentary on Surat al-Mu'minun.

**[Page 119]**

Ibn Abi Hatim recorded, via Abu Lahi'a from 'Abd al-Rahman al-A'raj, that he said concerning this smoke: it was on the day of the conquest of Makkah. And in the *Bahr* from him that he said: ﴿The day the sky brings﴾ and it is the day of the conquest of Makkah, when the sky was screened by dust. According to this view, it could well be a metonymy for what befell the people of Makkah on that day of fear, humiliation and the like.

'Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, Ibn 'Umar, Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, Zayd ibn 'Ali and al-Hasan said: It is a smoke that comes from the sky before the Day of Resurrection. It enters the ears of the disbelievers until the head of one of them is like a roasted head, and it affects the believer like the condition of a cold. The whole earth will be like a house that has been lit inside it, with no gaps.

Ibn Jarir recorded from Hudhayfa ibn al-Yaman, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), that: "The first of the signs is the Dajjal, the descent of 'Isa, and a fire that comes out from the bottom of Aden, driving people to the place of gathering; it rests with them when they rest, and [the smoke]." Hudhayfa said: O Messenger of Allah, and what is the smoke? Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited: ﴿So watch for the day the sky brings a clear smoke﴾, and said: It will fill what is between the east and the west. It will remain for forty days and nights. As for the believer, it will affect him like the condition of a cold, but as for the disbeliever, he will be like a drunkard, coming out of his nostrils, ears and rear. So the smoke is according to its apparent meaning, and the meaning is: watch for the day of the appearance of the smoke.

Al-Safarini related in *al-Buhur al-Zakhira*, from Ibn Mas'ud, that he used to say: "They are two smokes. One has passed, and the remaining one will fill what is between the sky and the earth. The believer will be affected only by a cold, but the disbeliever's hearing will be split. Then Allah Most High will send at that time the south wind from Yemen, which will seize the soul of every believer, and the wicked of people will remain." I do not think this narration from him is sound.

Taking what is in the verse to encompass both smokes is not hidden in its condition. It has been said: the meaning of "the day the sky brings" etc. is the Day of Resurrection, and the smoke may be intended to mean severity and evil, figuratively, or it may be intended literally.

Al-Khafaji said: The apparent reading of it is that His words, ﴿the sky brings﴾ to the end, are an allegorical metaphor (*isti'ara tamthiliyya*), since there is no sky, because it is a day on which the sky will be split. Its individual terms are in their literal meanings. You know that there is no obstacle to saying that the sky, as you heard at first, means the direction of height. Granting that it means the known body, there is nothing to prevent the smoke from being before its splitting, for example at the time when people come out of the graves. Indeed, there is no obstacle to saying that what is meant by the sky bringing smoke is its transformation into it after its splitting and its return to what it was at first, as He, glorified, said: ﴿Then He turned to the sky, and it was smoke﴾, and its annihilation would be after it becomes smoke.

That said, the more evident reading is to take the smoke as what was narrated from Ibn Mas'ud first, because it is more suitable to the context, since the passage concerns the disbelievers of Quraysh and the description of their evil condition. Moreover, the verses after it contain what is more fitting to it. The connection is that when He, glorified, mentioned their condition, namely that they met mercy with ingratitude and did not benefit from what was sent down and from the one upon whom it was sent down, He followed it with His words, exalted is His majesty, ﴿So watch for the day﴾ etc., to indicate that they are people of punishment and abandonment, not people of honour and forgiveness.

﴿Covering the people﴾, i.e., it envelops them. The intended people are the disbelievers of Quraysh. The clause is another attribute of "the smoke."

As for the words of the Exalted: ﴿This is a painful punishment.﴾ ﴿Our Lord, remove the punishment from us; indeed, we are believers.﴾ These are in a position of accusative case by an implied verb of saying, occurring as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning: saying, or they will say, "This is..." etc. The demonstrative is for magnification. It has also been said: it is permissible that "This is a painful punishment" be a statement from Him, Mighty and Majestic, to magnify the matter, as the Glorified and Exalted said in the story of the sacrificed one: ﴿Indeed, this is the manifest trial.﴾ In that case it is a resumptive (isti'nāf) or interjectory (i'tirāḍ) clause, and the demonstrative "this" indicates the nearness of its occurrence and its certainty. What preceded is more preferable. ﴿How can they [expect] to have the reminder [of faith]?﴾ This negates their sincerity in the promise, and that their aim is only the removal of the punishment and deliverance from it. Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 44, verse 14:

﴿Then they turned away from him﴾, i.e., from that Messenger, upon him be blessings and peace, and he is the same one. The matter is easier according to the view that it was at the conquest of Mecca, except that, nonetheless, it is not like the saying of Ibn Mas'ud. So reflect.

﴿On the day We seize with the greatest seizing﴾ is the Day of Badr, according to Ibn Mas'ud, and 'Abd ibn Humayd transmitted it. Ibn Jarir transmitted it from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Mujahid, al-Hasan, Abu al-'Aliyah, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Muhammad ibn Sirin, Qatada, and 'Atiyya. Ibn Mardawayh transmitted it from Ibn 'Abbas.

I say: it is the Day of Resurrection. In al-Bahr (al-Bahr al-Muhit, the commentary of Abu Hayyan) he reported, as a narration, that it is the Day of Resurrection, from al-Hasan and also from Qatada.

The adverbial phrase (al-zarf) is governed by what is indicated by the words of God Most High: ﴿Indeed We will take vengeance﴾. That is, "Indeed We will take vengeance on the day when Indeed We will take vengeance." It was also said that it is governed by ﴿muntaqimun﴾ (will take vengeance). Al-Zajjaj and others rejected this, on the ground that what follows inna (indeed) may not act upon what precedes it. It was also said that it is governed by ﴿la'a'idun﴾ (you will return), with the meaning: "Indeed you will return to the punishment on the day We seize."

It was also said that it is governed by ﴿kashifu al-'adhab﴾ (those who remove the punishment), but this is nothing. It was said that it is governed by "remember" (dhikrihim, or udhkur, understood as an implied verb). It was also said that it is a substitute (badal) for ﴿the Day the sky brings﴾, and so on.

It is read as (نَبْطُشُ) with a damma on the ta' (nabtush). al-Hasan, Abu Raja' and Talha, with a variant from him, read (نُبْطِشُ) with a damma on the nun, from the form of af'ala (the causative form), with the meaning: "We cause the angels, peace be upon them, to seize them, or We enable them to do so." The object is then omitted for knowledge of it and for added emphasis. On this reading, treating al-batshah (the seizing) as a absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq, a cognate object that emphasises the verbal noun) follows the pattern of ﴿anbatakum nabatan﴾ (who caused you to grow as a growth). Ibn Jinni and Abu Hayyan said: it is in the accusative governed by an implied verb indicated by the apparent verb, meaning: "the Day We seize whomever We seize, so he is seized with the greatest seizing." Ibn Jinni also said: "You may put it in the accusative as an object (maf'ul bihi), as if it were said: 'the Day We strengthen the greatest seizing against them and enable it over them,' as in your saying: 'the Day We empower killing against them and widen the taking from them.'"

In al-Qamus (the dictionary): "Batasha bihi, yabtishu, and yabtushu: he took him with violence and force, like abtashahu. Al-batsh is a severe seizing in everything, and it means might." End. So do not be negligent.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 44, verse 17:**

﴿And We had already tested the people of Pharaoh before them﴾. That is, We tested them by sending Musa (peace be upon him) to them. This may be taken as coming from "fatana al-fiḍḍah," meaning he placed the silver on the fire, so the word carries the sense of "testing." This is a *istiʿarah* (metaphor), and the meaning is that We dealt with them as one deals with someone being tested, so that their condition would become clear to others. Or it may be taken in its well-known meaning, that We put them into *fitnah* (trial). In that case, *fitnah* means that by which a person is tested, that is, he is deceived and heedless of what is good for him, as in His saying, ﴿Your wealth and your children are only a trial﴾. Here it has been explained as granting respite and widening provision.

Some have explained *fitnah* here as punishment, and then used it figuratively for the sins that cause it, which is burdening oneself with what one has no need for.

It is also read as *fattanna* with the *tāʾ* doubled. This is either to emphasize its verbal noun (*maṣdar*, the noun of action) meaning, or to intensify the object (*mafʿūl*) or the verb (*fiʿl*).

﴿And there came to them a noble Messenger﴾. That is, one honoured and esteemed by Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, or by the believers, or by Him and by them. Or he is *karīm* in himself, distinguished by praiseworthy qualities and noble attributes, in lineage and in descent.

Al-Raghib said: when *karam* (nobility) is attributed to a human being, it is a term for the praiseworthy morals and actions that appear from him, and one is not called *karīm* until that appears from him. It is transmitted from some scholars that *karam* is like *ḥarriyyah* (freedom of character), except that *ḥarriyyah* may be used for small and great virtues, while *karam* is used only for great virtues.

Al-Khafaji said: the original meaning of *karīm* is one who combines praiseworthy qualities and benefits. He claimed that explaining it this way is better than explaining it by the two previous explanations.

﴿Deliver to me the servants of God﴾: release them and hand them over to me. The intended meaning is the Children of Israel, whom Pharaoh had enslaved. Referring to them as "the servants of God" (ʿibād Allāh) indicates that his enslaving them was an injustice on his part. The word "deliver" (adāʾ) is used metaphorically for what has been mentioned. This is like his saying, peace be upon him: ﴿Send the Children of Israel with us and do not torment them﴾. This was related from Ibn Zayd, Mujahid and Qatadah.

Or it means: ﴿deliver to me the right of God Most High﴾, namely faith and the acceptance of the call, "O servants of God." On this reading the object of (adʰū, "deliver") is omitted, and "servants" (ʿibād) is a vocative (munādā, addressed noun), and it is general, covering both the Children of Israel and the Copts. Here "deliver" (adāʾ) carries the sense of "obey" (al-fiʿl lil-ṭāʿa) and "accept the call." This was related from Ibn Abbas.

As for the word "that" (an) in both cases, it is said to be a verbal (maṣdariyya) particle, with a preceding prepositional particle (ḥarf jarr) implied, linked to "came to them" (jāaʾahum), meaning "with [the command] that: deliver." This has been objected to: there is no sense in your saying "he came to them with the delivery to me," and interpreting it as a demand for delivery to me is not free from strain. It has been answered that it is by implication of "saying" (al-qawl), which is common and regular, so its implied form is "that he said: deliver to me." Yet this is not free from some artificiality. Moreover, this command is based on the permissibility of joining the verbal "that" to an imperative or prohibitive, which is not agreed upon. Indeed, the more correct view is that it is permissible.

It has also been said that it is the lightened form (mukhaffafa) of the heavy one (al-thaqīla). This has been objected to: in that case an implied pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-shaʾn) would be assumed before it, and its explaining element (mufassir) must be only a declarative sentence (jumla khabariyya). Also, after it there must be either a negation, or "qad," or the future marker "sa-" or "sawfa," or "law," and it must be preceded by a verb of the heart or the like. It was answered that the coming of the messenger implies the sense of a verb of affirmation, such as "informing." The aforementioned condition is not agreed upon: al-Mubarrad, following the Baghdadis, held that it is not required. The claim that this is an anomaly (shādh), from which the Qur'an must be protected, is not accepted. The condition that the explaining element of the implied pronoun of the matter must be a declarative sentence is subject to dispute, as is understood from the words of some scholars. In al-Mughni (Ibn Hisham), in the fourth chapter on the implied pronoun of the matter, only the condition that its explaining element be a sentence is mentioned, without the condition of it being declarative, and no disagreement is noted. However, in the fifth chapter he said: "The eighth type: the stipulation for some sentences to be declarative and for others to be imperative. Among the first type he counted the two predicates of 'anna' and the pronoun of the matter. But he then said: 'It should be excepted from this, in the two predicates of anna and the pronoun of the matter, the predicate of the opening-'anna' when lightened; it may be a supplicatory sentence, as in God's saying: ﴿and the fifth [oath is] that the wrath of God be upon her﴾, according to the reading of whoever reads 'an' and 'ghadiba' (with the verb), with the Majestic Name as the subject."

Some eminent scholars verified that the report about the implied pronoun of the matter by an imperative sentence is permissible according to al-Zamakhshari, or that it is explanatory, and that what indicates the speech without its letters has already been mentioned, because the coming of the messenger is with a message and a call. It is as if the explanation is of its implied complement, meaning: he came to them with the call, which is: ﴿deliver to me, servants of God﴾, ﴿I am to you a trustworthy messenger﴾, ﴿and do not exalt yourselves against God﴾, and do not behave arrogantly toward Him, glorified be He, by treating His revelation and His messenger, peace be upon him, with contempt. The word ﴿that﴾ is like the one before it. The meaning, on the verbal reading, is: by restraining yourselves from exalting yourselves against God Most High. ﴿I am bringing you a clear authority﴾ is a reason for the prohibition: that is, I am bringing you a clear proof that cannot be denied, or one that makes clear the truth of my claim. The verb "I am bringing" (ātīkum) may be read in the form of the active participle or the imperfect. The fine appropriateness of mentioning "trustworthy" together with "delivery," and "authority" together with "exaltation," is evident. It has been mentioned that the first contains a development (tarshīḥ) of the explicit or implicit metaphor, by making them as if they were property belonging to another, in whose hand it lies, commanded to hand it over to whoever is entrusted with it. The second contains an equivocation (tawriya) about the meaning of "king," supported by the phrase ﴿do not exalt yourselves﴾.

A group read "innī" (with a kasra on the hamza) with a fatha on the hamza, that is, "annī." It has been said that this too is a reason for the prohibition, with the preposition lām implied. It has also been said that it is connected to what the prohibition was applied to, like your saying to someone who was angry at a truth told to him: "Do not be angry, because the truth has been told to you."

﴿So they shall not reach you﴾. The clause is a conjunction with the resumptive clause [preceding it]. Abu 'Amr and the two Akhawan [i.e., al-Kisa'i and Hamza... ] read ʿuttu (عُتُّ) with the assimilation of the dhal into the ta'.

﴿And if you do not believe me, then keep away from me.﴾ So be at a distance from me, neither against me nor for me, and do not harm me, for that is not the recompense of one who calls you to that in which your salvation lies. It has also been said: the meaning is, "If you do not believe in me, then there is no friendship between me and one who does not believe, so withdraw and cut off the ties of connection with me." In this case the response is omitted from the speech, and the cause is put in the place of its effect. The first interpretation is more suitable to the context. Withdrawal (i'tizal) here is an expression for abandonment, even if it is not a physical separation of bodies.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 44, verse 22:

﴿So he called upon his Lord﴾ after they had persisted in denying him, peace be upon him, ﴿that these are a guilty people﴾. That is, "that these people..." and so on. Thus the preposition (the bāʾ, "with/that") is understood as attached to the verb of calling, just as one says "he called with this supplication" (daʿā bi-hādhā al-duʿāʾ). There is an ellipsis here, as if it were said: "These are a guilty people; their affair in disbelief has reached its extreme, and You know them best, so do to them what they deserve." It was said that his supplication, peace be upon him, was: "O Allah, hasten for them what they deserve for their crimes." And it was said: his saying ﴿O our Lord, do not make us a trial for the wrongdoing people﴾ up to His saying ﴿so they will not believe until they see the painful punishment﴾ [cf. Q. 10:85–88]. Allah, glory be to Him, mentioned the cause that made them deserve destruction so that it may be known from it both his supplication and the answer together, and that his supplication was made in despair of their faith. This is among the eloquent abbreviations of the miraculous Book.

Ibn Abi Ishaq, ʿĪsā, al-Ḥasan in one narration, and Zayd ibn ʿAlī read the hamza of ﴿inna﴾ with a kasra. It is construed as implying a verb of saying, i.e., "saying: indeed these people..." (qā'ilan inna hā'ulā' ilakh).

﴿So travel by night with My servants﴾, who are the Children of Israel and those among the Copts who believed in him. ﴿By night﴾, that is, during a portion of the night. The speech is one in which a verb of saying is implied (idmar al-qawl, the implied verb of speaking). It may come after the فاء (fa'), meaning: so he said, "Travel, etc." Here the فاء indicates sequence and order (lit-ta'qib wa al-tartib). The verb of saying is then coordinated with what precedes it, or with the particle before it, as if it were said: "He said." Or it may mean: "So he said, 'If the matter is as you say, then travel, etc.'" In that case the فاء falls in the answer of an implied conditional clause (shart muqaddar), and the answer together with the فاء (or without it, taken as a new independent sentence, isti'naf) is the quoted speech that is implied. The first implication is preferable, because implying less is better, and because the implication of أن (an) does not suit this context, since there is no doubt about it, either in reality or as a presumption. Taking the فاء to mean إذا (idha, "when") is an excessive stretch upon a stretch. Abu Hayyan does not permit omitting the conditional clause while retaining its answer in such a position, and he severely criticized al-Zamakhshari for permitting it. Nafi' and Ibn Kathir read فاسْرِ with the hamza of wasl (elided hamza), from سرى (sara).

﴿Indeed you will be pursued﴾: Pharaoh and his soldiers will follow you when they learn of your departure. The sentence is therefore a new independent sentence (mustaʼnafa), giving the reason for the command to travel by night, so that knowledge of it is delayed and they will not overtake you. The emphasis (ta'kid) is for the sake of what is hinted at beforehand by the news (li-taqaddum ma yalluh bi-al-khabar).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 44, verse 24:

﴿And leave the sea parted﴾, i.e., still, as Ibn 'Abbas said. It is said: "raha al-bahr yarhu rahwan" meaning it became still (saakana). It is also said: "jaa'at al-khayl rahwan," meaning the horses came in a calm (saakinah) manner. The poet said:

"And the horses, in their bridles, glide rahwan
like birds escaping the downpour of hail"

It is also said: "if'al dhalika rahwan," meaning do that calmly, in a gentle manner. More than one transmitter recited, for the description of riding beasts, a verse of al-Qutami:

"They walk rahwan, neither their hindquarters failing
nor their chests relying upon the hindquarters"

The apparent meaning is that it is originally a verbal noun (masdar) interpreted as an active participle (ism al-fa'il). It is also permissible that it means "still" in its literal sense. From Mujahid: rahwan means open and wide. Abu 'Ubaydah said: "raha al-rajul yarhu rahwan," meaning he spread his legs apart. From some Arabs: he saw a camel that was fali, i.e., having two humps, and said: "Glory be to God the Exalted, rahwun between two humps." They said: he meant a wide gap.

The apparent meaning is also that it is a verbal noun interpreted as such, or that there is an implied genitive, i.e., "possessing a gap." Qatadah said: after Musa, peace be upon him, and those with him had crossed the sea, he wanted to strike it with his staff so that it would rejoin as it had when he struck it first and it split, lest Pharaoh and his hosts follow them. He was commanded to leave it rahwan, i.e., open and parted, or still in its state, remaining as it is regarding the standing of the water and the path being dry, and not striking it with his staff nor changing anything of it, so that the Copts would enter it. When they were within it, Allah the Exalted would close it over them. This is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed they are a host to be drowned﴾. So this is the reason for the command to leave it rahwan. It was said: rahwan means easy; it was said: dry; it was said: smooth paths; it was said: other than that. All of these are explanations of the resulting meaning.

Al-Raghib claimed that the correct view is that rahw means a wide road; then he said: from it comes al-rahaa', a level desert, and every level basin in which water gathers is called rahw. From it it is said: there is no pre-emption (shufah) in rahw. The truth is that what he mentioned is among its usages, but as for it being the correct one, that is not so.

It was also read as (annahum) with a fatha, meaning because they...

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 44, verses 25–26:

﴿How many they left behind﴾ That is, they left behind much of ﴿gardens and springs﴾ ﴿and crops and a noble station﴾, meaning good and honourable in its kind. By this is meant, as related from Qatadah, the fine places of gatherings and dwellings and other things.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn ʿAbbas, and Ibn Mardawayh from Jabir, that what is meant is the pulpits (manabir). This is also related from Mujahid and Ibn Jubayr. It was said: the couches (sururs) in the canopied enclosures (hijal). The first view is preferable.

Ibn Hurmuz, Qatadah, Ibn al-Samaiqa and Nafi' (in the transmission of Kharijah) read (muqamin) with a ḍammah on the mim.
