**[Verse 27]: ﴿ونَعْمَةٍ﴾** means *tana"‘um* (ease and luxury). Al-Raghib said: *al-ni‘mah* with a fatha (*al-na‘mah*) means *al-tana‘‘um* (luxury), and its form is *bina’ al-marrah* (the form denoting a single instance of the verbal action, like *al-darbah* "a blow" and *al-shatmah* "an insult"). *Al-ni‘mah* with a kasra (*al-ni‘mah*) means *al-halah al-hasanah* (a good state), and its form is *bina’ al-hay’ah* (the form denoting the manner in which a person is, like *al-jilsah* "a manner of sitting" and *al-rikbah* "a manner of riding"). It is used for a genus that applies to both little and much. Interpreting *al-ni‘mah* here as "the thing bestowed" was preferred, because it is more suitable to *al-tark* (leaving behind), and it often carries this meaning.

Abu Raja’ read ﴿ونَعْمَةً﴾ with a fatha. It has been explained as being in the accusative by coordination with ﴿كَمْ﴾ (how many). It was also said that it is coordinated with the place (*mahall*) of what precedes it, as if it were said:

"How many they left of gardens, springs, crops, a noble station, and luxury ﴿they had been therein merry﴾, joyful in their souls, and possessors of fruit, so *fakih* is like *laabin* and *tamir*." Al-Qushayri said: "*lahin*" (heedless). Al-Hasan and Abu Raja’ read ﴿فَكِهِينَ﴾ without an alif. *Al-fakih* is frequently used for one who is light-hearted and mocking, so the meaning is: those who were making light of thankfulness for the blessing they were in.

Al-Jawhari said: *fakiha al-rajul* with a kasra (*fakiha*) means he is *fakih*, if he is *mazzah* (a jester, one who jokes a great deal). *Al-fakih* also means *al-ashir* (exultant, insolent with pride).

﴿Thus﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is "the matter is thus," and the purpose is emphasis and affirmation, so one stops at that point. The kaf (ك) is then in the position of the predicate of an omitted subject, or the prepositional phrase "thus" is what is meant. It has also been said that the kaf is in the accusative position, meaning: We do an act like this to whoever We wish to destroy. Al-Kalbi's statement, "That is, thus do I deal with those who disobey Me," is clearly consistent with what has been mentioned. Al-Zamakhshari said: the kaf is in the accusative position in the sense of "like that removal," that is, what is understood from what preceded, that We removed them from it. ﴿And We made other people inherit them﴾ is coordinated with "they left behind," and the sentence is a parenthetical insertion in every view except the last one, and in the view that the kaf refers to "We removed them." It has also been said that the kaf is in the accusative position in the sense of "they left behind a departure like that," so the coordination is with ﴿they left behind﴾ without any parenthetical insertion. This, as you see, is weak. By "other people" is meant the Children of Israel, and they are distinct from the Copts in lineage and religion. This is explained by the verse in Surat al-Shu'ara': ﴿Thus; and We made the Children of Israel inherit it﴾, which clearly indicates that the Children of Israel returned to Egypt after the destruction of Pharaoh and possessed it. Al-Hasan also held this view.

It has been said that the intended people are other than the Children of Israel, namely those who ruled Egypt after the destruction of the Copts. Qatada held this view and said: it is not reported in well-known histories that the Children of Israel returned to Egypt or that they ever ruled it. He interpreted the verse in Surat al-Shu'ara' as falling under the category of ﴿No one is granted a long life, nor is anything taken from his lifespan﴾ and of your saying, "I have a dirham and half of it." So the intended meaning is not specifically what they left behind, [p. 124] but its kind and what resembles it. Inheritance (al-iratha) means giving. It has been said that by their inheriting it is meant that they were enabled to dispose of it, and this does not depend on their returning to Egypt as they had been there at first. A group followed al-Hasan's view and said: there is no weight to the histories, nor to the books in the hands of the Jews today, since falsehood is abundant in them. "The Book of Allah is sufficient for us," and He, glorified is He, is the most truthful of speakers, and His Book, exalted is He, is protected from the distortion of distorters.

﴿فَما بَكَتْ عَلَيْهِمُ السَّماءُ والأرْضُ﴾ ﴿So the sky and the earth did not weep for them﴾ is a figurative expression (majaz) for not caring about their destruction and not regarding their existence as significant. It is a metaphorical image (istiʿarah tamthiliyyah, a metaphor drawn from a whole scene) and imaginative (takhyiliyyah). It likens the state of their death, because of its severity and magnitude, to the state of someone over whom the sky and the great celestial bodies weep, and it attributes that weeping to them. The negation follows the affirmation in the figurative usage, as has been verified in its proper place. It has also been said that it is an implicit metaphor (istiʿarah makniyyah) that is imaginative, by likening the sky and the earth to a human being and attributing weeping to them, or a metaphorical image, by likening their condition, in that they do not change and remain as they were, to the condition of one who does not weep. But this is not correct, as will be clear to anyone who consults their words. It has been common in glorifying the death of a person to say that the sky and the earth wept over him, or that the wind wept for him, and similar expressions. Yazid ibn Mufarrigh said:

The wind weeps for his grief, and the lightning flashes within its cloud.

And al-Nabigha said:

Harith al-Jolan wept for the loss of his lord, and Hauran was humbled and bowed down because of him.

He meant by these two names two known places. Jarir said:

When the news of al-Zubayr came, the walls of Madinah and the humbled mountains humbled themselves.

And al-Farazdaq, lamenting Amir al-Mu'minin Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz, said:

The sun rises, not eclipsed, weeping for you, and the stars of the night and the moon.

He is marveling at the rising of the sun, when it should by rights not rise, or should rise eclipsed. The word "stars" (nujum) is narrated in both the accusative and the nominative. The accusative is in the sense of contention (al-mughalabah), meaning that the sun outdoes the stars in weeping, as in the phrase "baka'tuhu fa-bakaytuhu" (I wept with him and outdid him in weeping). Jar Allah (al-Zamakhshari) said: He, may Allah be pleased with him, used to pray at night, so the stars wept for him; and he used to act justly during the day, so the sun wept for him, and the sun was the greater in weeping, because justice is better than night prayer. Al-Jawhari (ʿAbd Allah ibn Hammad al-Jawhari) made it accusative with "kasifah" (eclipsed), meaning that it does not eclipse the light of the stars because of its abundant weeping. It seems he took the concealment of the stars beneath the light of the sun to be an eclipse for them, figuratively. However, in this interpretation the meaning of eclipse as stated is not clear, and the phrase "tabki" (weeping) with its intervening element is not eloquent. In the margins of al-Sihah it says: "The sun is eclipsed, not rising." In it there is also that "nujum al-layl" (the stars of the night) is a time expression (zarf), meaning throughout the duration of the night, as if it were from the pattern of "ātīka al-shamsa wa al-qamar" (I will come to you at sunrise and moonrise), meaning at the time of them both, as if it were said: she weeps for the time when the stars and the moon rise. But in this there is that such a time expression is heard only rarely and is not established except by a firm reliance, so how can one turn to it when the clear meaning is available? It has been said that the implied construction is "tabki buka'a al-nujum" (she weeps with the weeping of the stars), and the genitive term has been omitted. But in this there is that it is something that is hardly understood. The nominative reading is clear, and "al-qamar" (the moon) is in the accusative as an object of accompaniment (maf'ul maʿah). This digression was prompted by the fame of the line together with the great confusion surrounding it.

Al-Tirmidhi and a group of others narrated from Anas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "There is no servant but that he has two doors in the sky: a door through which his deed ascends, and a door through which his provision descends. When the believer dies, they both miss him and weep for him." Then he recited this verse: ﴿So the sky and the earth did not weep for them﴾, and he mentioned that they (the disbelievers) had not done any righteous deed on the face of the earth, so it would not miss them and weep for them, and that no good word or righteous deed had ascended to the sky from their speech or their deeds, so it would not miss them and weep for them.

Al-Bayhaqi in Shuʿab al-Iman, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and others narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: "The earth weeps for the believer for forty mornings." Then he recited the verse. Ibn al-Mundhir and others narrated from Ali, may Allah honor his face, that he said: "When the believer dies, his place of prayer on the earth weeps for him, and the ascent of his deed in the sky weeps for him." Then he recited ﴿So they did not weep﴾ and so on. They all considered all of this to be of the category of imaginative representation (tamthil).

As for one who affirms, as the Sufis do, for the celestial and earthly bodies and all other inanimate things a consciousness suited to their condition, there is no need to consider this as a representation, and he affirms for them a real weeping in accordance with what their essence requires and what befits them. Or he interprets it as sorrow or something similar, and affirms it for them accordingly.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ata: "The weeping of the sky is the redness of its horizons." Ibn Abi al-Dunya narrated from al-Hasan something similar. He also narrated from Sufyan al-Thawri, who said: It was said: "This redness that appears in the sky is the weeping of the sky over the believer." By my life, whoever does not laugh at this should weep over his own intellect. I do not believe that those mentioned among the eminent ones held this view. It has been said that the verse is according to an implied construction, meaning: "So the inhabitants of the sky did not weep for them," that is, the angels, "and the inhabitants of the earth," that is, the believers, "did not weep for them. Rather, they were rejoicing at their destruction."

This was also narrated from al-Hasan, but the best view is the one previously mentioned. ﴿And they were not﴾, when the time of their destruction came, ﴿given respite﴾, that is, granted delay until another time, or until the Day of Resurrection, "but rather they were hastened to it in this world."

Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on surah 44, verses 30–31:

﴿And We had certainly delivered the Children of Israel﴾ from what We did to Pharaoh and his people, ﴿from the humiliating torment﴾, namely the enslavement by Pharaoh, his slaughtering of their sons, and his sparing of their women, along with the degradation and oppression. ﴿From Pharaoh﴾ is a *badal* (substitute, in apposition) for "the torment", with the governed noun omitted, so that the sense is "from the torment of Pharaoh". Or [the author] took it to mean that the torment itself is Pharaoh, as an intensifying exaggeration. It was also permitted that it be connected to an omitted element functioning as a circumstantial qualifier (*hal*), meaning "coming from the direction of Pharaoh". It was also said that it is connected to an omitted element functioning as a qualifier (*sifa*), meaning "being from Pharaoh" or "the one from Pharaoh". There is no harm in this, provided it does not amount to omitting the relative pronoun together with part of its clause.

ʿAbd Allāh read *min ʿadhābi al-muhīn* ("from the torment of the humiliating one"), taking the modified noun as genitive of its qualifier, like the expression *baqlat al-ḥamqāʾ* ("the purslane of the foolish one"). Ibn ʿAbbās read *man* (فِرْعَوْنُ), with *Fir'awn* in the nominative, as an interrogative, to magnify the torment, meaning: do you know who Pharaoh is in his insolence and tyranny? So what do you suppose his torment to be? It was also said that it is to belittle Pharaoh by making him unknown, so that one asks about him as one asks about an indefinite noun, because of the abominable deeds attributed to him which had no precedent. What follows fits what precedes, as is not hidden.

In any case, the apparent view is that the sentence is a new resumptive clause (*istiʾnaf*). It was also said that it is a quoted statement of an implied saying, which is a qualifier of the torment. The quoted statement is to be understood as implied in this view, and if the definite article in "the torment" is for a specific reference (*ʿahd*), the quoted statement is specific; if it is for the genus (*jins*), it is general. So do not overlook this. ﴿Indeed he was haughty﴾, arrogant, ﴿of the extravagant﴾, in wrongdoing and corruption. The prepositional phrase ("of the extravagant") is either a second predicate of *kāna* (was), meaning "he was arrogant, immersed in extravagance", or a circumstantial qualifier (*hal*) from the pronoun concealed in *ʿāliyan* (haughty), meaning "he was arrogant while immersed in extravagance".

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 44, verse 32:

﴿And We certainly chose them﴾, i.e., We chose the Children of Israel and honoured them, ﴿over knowledge﴾, i.e., knowing their worthiness of that, or together with knowledge from Us of what they fall short in at some times. It was also said: knowing what proceeds from them of justice, goodness, knowledge and faith. This returns to what was said first, for justice and what accompanies it are among the causes of worthiness. It was also said: ﴿over knowledge﴾ means for the sake of a knowledge that is in them. This was objected to as weak, because the indefiniteness of "knowledge" does not match its intended meaning.

It was answered that the indefiniteness is for magnification, and it is fitting to consider it a cause of the choosing. ﴿over the worlds﴾, i.e., the worlds of their time, as Mujahid and Qatadah said. The definite article is then for a specific reference (ʿahd) or for customary generality (istighraq ʿurfi), so it does not necessarily follow that they are preferred over the Ummah of Muhammad (ﷺ), who are ﴿the best community brought forth for mankind﴾, [Qur'an 3:110], absolutely. It was also permitted that it be for true generality (istighraq haqiqi) and preference with respect to the great number of prophets (peace be upon them) among them, not in every respect, so that it would not follow that they are preferred over this Muhammadan Ummah. It was also said: the meaning is "We chose them" as an indication of the manner in which it occurred and that We singled them out for it over the worlds, but this is not correct.

From what we have mentioned it is known that the verse does not contain two prepositions (ḥarfay jarr) with a single meaning attached to one governing word, because the first is attached to an omitted element that falls as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), and the second is attached to the verb, as in the saying of the poet:

﴿and one day upon the sand-dune, she made it impossible for me, and an oath was sworn that could not be undone﴾

It was also said: this is because every preposition has a meaning.

And We gave them of the signs that which contained a clear trial (blaʾ mubin). Al-Alusi writes: ﴿And We gave them of the signs﴾ such as the splitting of the sea, the shading of them by the cloud, and the sending down of the manna and the quails, and other great signs, the like of which was not known among others. And some of them, although Moses (peace be upon him) was given them too, it is true of them that they were given them, because what belongs to the Prophet belongs to his nation. ﴿That which contained a clear trial﴾, meaning a manifest blessing or a manifest test, to see how they would act. In (fihi), "in it", there is an indication that there are other matters, such as its being a miracle.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 44, verses 34–35:

﴿Indeed, these﴾ refers to the disbelievers of Quraysh, since the discussion concerns them. The mention of the story of Pharaoh and his people is a digression (istitradi) to show that they are similar to them in their persistence in misguidance and in being warned against what befell those peoples. The demonstrative pronoun also carries a sense of belittling them. ﴿They say﴾ ﴿There is only our first death﴾, meaning: the final outcome and end of the matter is only the first death, which ends the worldly life. ﴿And we will not be resurrected﴾, meaning: we will not be raised again after it. Describing it as "first" is not meant to contrast it with a second, as in your saying: "Zayd performed the first pilgrimage (ḥajj) and died."

Al-Isnawi said in al-Tamhid: "The first (al-awwal) in language is the beginning of a thing. Then it may or may not have a second. For example, you say: 'This is the first thing I acquired,' and you may then acquire something after it or you may not." This was mentioned by a group of scholars, including al-Wahidi in his tafsir and al-Zajjaj.

Among the branches of this issue is that if a man says: "If the first child you bear is a male, then you are divorced," she is divorced when she gives birth to him, and if she bears no other child, this is agreed upon. Abu Ali said: "They agreed that it is not a condition of being first that another should come after it; the condition is only that no other precedes it." End of quote. From this, the error in the statement of some of them is known, that "the first" necessarily implies "the second" and requires its existence without doubt. The example, if it is correct, applies only to one who intended to perform the pilgrimage multiple times but was overtaken by death, so his second pilgrimage exists by way of intention, owing to a deficiency in knowledge. There is no need to say that it is "first" relative to what comes after it of the life of the Hereafter. Indeed, this in itself is unacceptable, for Ibn al-Munir said that the "first" is only opposed by an "other" (ukhrā) that shares its most specific meanings. Just as it is not valid, or not proper, to say: "A man came to me and another woman," it is not said "the first death" in relation to the life of the Hereafter.

It was also said that they were told: "You will die one death which will be followed by a life, just as a death preceded you which was followed by a life." This is His statement, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿You were dead and He gave you life; then He will cause you to die, then He will give you life again﴾. Then they said: ﴿There is only our first death﴾, meaning: the death which is of the kind that is followed by life is only the first death and not the second. And this attribute you ascribe to death, that it is followed by life, applies only to the first death specifically. This is what Jar Allah (al-Zamakhshari) approved, and he held that the negation and affirmation, since they were meant to bring the stubborn denier back to the truth, are directed at their denial. Especially since the definite article in "al-ūlā" is the definite article of prior reference (ta'rif 'ahd). His statement, exalted is He: ﴿the first death﴾, is an explanation of the ambiguous term, and it is like the Arabs' saying: "So-and-so says such-and-such," so the two agree. The known meaning is the death that is followed by the worldly life. For this reason he cited His statement: ﴿You were dead﴾ and so on. Thus, treating the attribute as a departure from the apparent meaning without need is not valid, as Ibn al-Munir said.

As for his statement in the objection as well: that the death preceding the worldly life is not expressed by "death once" (mawtah), because "in it" (fīhā), due to the pattern of the single instance (ism al-marrah), indicates renewal, and the preceding death is continuous and was not preceded by a life, is rejected, as the author of al-Kashshaf said. Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 44, verse 37 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Are they better﴾ in strength and might, ﴿or the people of Tubba'﴾, who is Tubba' al-Akbar (the Greatest) al-Himyari, whose name is As'ad (with a hamzah), though in some books it is Sa'd without it; his kunyah is Abu Karib, and he was a righteous man. Al-Hakim narrated and authenticated (it) from A'ishah, who said: "Tubba' was a righteous man. Do you not see that Allah the Exalted censured his people but did not censure him?" Ibn 'Asakir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas: "Let not the matter of Tubba' be confused for you, for he was a Muslim." Ahmad, al-Tabarani, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Sahl ibn Sa'd al-Sa'idi, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Do not revile Tubba', for he had embraced Islam.'" Ibn 'Asakir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "I asked Ka'b about Tubba', for I hear Allah the Exalted mention in the Qur'an the people of Tubba' but not Tubba' himself." He said: "Tubba' was a man from the people of Yemen, a victorious king. He marched with armies until he reached Samarqand, then he returned and took the road to Syria, and he took captive some rabbis from there and set off with them towards Yemen. When he approached his kingdom, it spread among the people that he intended to demolish the Ka'bah. The rabbis said to him: 'What is this that you are contemplating in yourself? This House belongs to Allah the Exalted, and you will not be given power over it.' He said: 'This belongs to Allah the Exalted, and I am most entitled to honour it.' So he embraced Islam on the spot, entered Ihram, and entered it (Makkah) in the state of Ihram, completed his rites, then turned back towards Yemen, until he came to his people. Their nobles entered upon him and said: 'O Tubba', you are our master and the son of our master. You left us upon one religion and came back upon another. Choose from us one of two matters: either you leave us and our kingdom and worship whatever you wish, or you abandon the religion you have introduced.' Between them on that day there was a fire descending from the sky. The rabbis then said: 'Make the fire between you and them.' The people all agreed to make it between them. The rabbis and their books were brought, and the idols and their attendants were brought, and they were all brought forward to the fire, while men stood behind them with swords. The fire roared like thunder and cast forth its flame; the idol-worshippers recoiled, and the fire advanced and burned the idols and their attendants, and the others were spared. Some embraced Islam and some submitted. They remained thus for the lifetime of Tubba'. When death came upon Tubba', he appointed his brother as successor and died. They killed his brother and disbelieved together in one stroke." 

In another narration from Ibn 'Abbas: when Tubba' came from the east, after he had built al-Hirah, that is, founded it and organised its affairs. It is with a kasrah on the ha' (unpointed) and a silent ya', a city near Kufa.

He built Samarqand, which is a well-known city in Persia (al-'Ajam). It is also said that he demolished it and then headed for Madinah, having left behind there a son who was killed by treachery; so he resolved to ruin it and uproot its people. The Ansar gathered against him and went out to fight him; they fought him by day and hosted him by night. This pleased him, and he said: "These are indeed noble people." While he was in this state, two rabbis, Ka'b and Asad, sons of a paternal uncle, from Quraizah, came to him and informed him that he would be prevented from what he wished, "for it is the place of emigration of a Prophet from Quraysh named Muhammad (ﷺ), whose birth is in Makkah." Their words diverted him from what he intended; then they invited him to their religion, and he followed them and honoured them. They turned away from Madinah, with a group of Jews accompanying them. A group from Hudhayl said to him on the road: "We will guide you to a house in Makkah containing a treasure of pearls, emeralds, gold and silver." Hudhayl intended his destruction, for they knew that whoever intended harm to him would perish. He mentioned that to the two rabbis, and they said: "We know of no house on earth that Allah the Mighty and Majestic has taken for Himself other than this one. So take it as a mosque, sacrifice there, shave your head, and the people intend nothing but your destruction." So he honoured it and clothed it, and he was the first to clothe the House. He cut off the hands and feet of those men of Hudhayl, put out their eyes and crucified them. In another narration, when the two rabbis said to him what they said, he asked: "And what prevents you two from doing that?" They replied: "By Allah, it is the House of our father Ibrahim, peace be upon him, and what we told you is true; but its people have stood between us and it with the idols they set up around it and the blood they pour out at it, and they are impure idolaters." He recognised their truthfulness and accepted their advice. He circumambulated the House, sacrificed, shaved his head, and remained in Makkah for six days, according to what they report, slaughtering for the people and feeding its inhabitants and giving them honey to drink. It is also said that he intended to destroy the House, but he was struck with a great affliction, so he desisted and clothed it.
Ibn 'Asakir narrated from Ibn Ishaq that Tubba' was shown in a dream that he should clothe the House; so he clothed it with khasf (woven palm-fibre matting). Then he was shown that he should clothe it with something better than that, so he clothed it with ma'afir; then he was shown that he should clothe it with something better still, so he clothed it with wasa'il and sail of Yemen. It was mentioned to me that he was the first to clothe it, and he bequeathed (this) to his governors from Jurhum, and he ordered it to be purified, and he made for it a door and a key. In another narration he also said: "Do not bring blood near it, nor a corpse, and let no menstruating woman approach it." In Ibn al-Athir's Nihayah, in a hadith, Tubba' clothed the House with coarse garments (masuh), so the House shook and tore them off from itself; then he clothed it with khasf and it did not accept it; then he clothed it with antla'. Elsewhere in it: the first to clothe the Ka'bah with a complete covering was Tubba'; he clothed it with antla', then with wasa'il and khasf. Khasf is a verbal noun in the sense of a passive participle, from al-khasf, which is joining one thing to another; the intended meaning is, as is apparent, something woven from palm-fibre; it is also said that what is meant here is garments very coarse, likened to the aforementioned khasf. Ma'afir are striped Yemeni cloths named after Ma'afir, a tribe there, the mim being extra. Wasa'il are red striped Yemeni garments. Masuh is the plural of misḥ (with a kasrah on the mim and a silent unpointed letter), thick hair garments. Antla' is the plural of niṭa' (with kasrah, fathah, or fathah with the middle letter vowelled), spreads of leather.
Ibn Sa'd and Ibn 'Asakir narrated from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, who said: When Tubba' came to Madinah and camped at its outskirts, he sent for the rabbis of the Jews and said: "I will ruin this city so that no Jew will remain in it, and the matter will return to the religion of the Arabs." Shamul the Jew, who was then the most knowledgeable of them, said to him: "O King, this is a land which will be the place of emigration of a Prophet from the sons of Isma'il, born in Makkah, named Ahmad, and this is the abode of his emigration..." He said: "And what is his description?" He said: "A man neither short nor tall, with redness in his eyes, who rides a camel and wears a shamlah, his sword upon his shoulder, who fears no one he meets until his affair becomes manifest." Tubba' said: "There is no way to this city, and its ruin would not be at my hands."
Abu Hatim al-Riyashi mentioned that he believed in the Prophet (ﷺ) seven hundred years before he was sent. Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Say nothing about Tubba' but good, for he performed Hajj to the House and believed in what 'Isa ibn Maryam brought." This indicates that he was after the mission of 'Isa (peace be upon him); but the first is more well-known.

I have been told that the Messenger of the King will truly emerge in the land of the Sanctuary,
If my life were extended to his time, I would be his minister and cousin.
In al-Bahr, in place of the first verse:
I bear witness regarding Ahmad that he is a Messenger from Allah, Creator of souls.
In it also is a report from Ibn Ishaq and others that he also wrote a letter, in which was: "To proceed: I have believed in you and in your Book which was sent down to you, and I am upon your religion and your sunnah, and I have believed in your Lord and the Lord of all things, and I have believed in all that has come from your Lord of the laws of Islam. If I attain you, then it is well; and if I do not attain you, then intercede for me and do not forget me on the Day of Resurrection, for I am of your first community and your followers before your coming, and I am upon your creed and the creed of your father Ibrahim, peace be upon him." Then he sealed the letter and engraved upon it: "To Allah belongs the command, before and after," and he wrote its address: "To Muhammad ibn 'Abdullah, the Prophet of Allah and His Messenger, the Seal of the Prophets and Messenger of the Lord of the Worlds (ﷺ), from Tubba' the First," and he handed it to a notable of the Aws and the Khazraj, instructing him to deliver it to the Prophet (peace be upon him) if he attained him.
It is said that he built a house for him in Madinah in which he would stay when he attained the Prophet (ﷺ) and came to it; and that this house is the house of Abu Ayyub Khalid ibn Zayd; and that the poetry and the letter reached him, and that he is a descendant of that man to whom they were first handed. When the Prophet (peace be upon him) became manifest, they handed the letter to him; when it was read to him, he said: "Welcome, Tubba' the righteous brother," three times.
It is reported that the Prophet (ﷺ) prayed the funeral prayer over him, and likewise over al-Bara' ibn Ma'rur a month after his death, on the day of his arrival at Madinah, as al-Najm al-Ghaytі said; and the funeral prayer had been enjoined that year. As for this being Tubba' the First, who is called al-Akbar, it is what is mentioned in more than one book. 'Abd al-Malik ibn 'Abdullah ibn Badrun mentioned in his commentary on the qasidah of Ibn 'Abdun that this As'ad is Tubba' al-Awsat (the Middle), and he also mentioned that his reign was three hundred and twenty years, and after him 'Amr reigned sixty-four years. Ibn Qutaybah said: Hassan, who killed Zarqa' al-Yamamah and annihilated Judays, and his reign was twenty-five years. The histories are clear that the Tababi'ah preceded him, for Tubba' is said of whoever rules Yemen absolutely, as Khaqan is said of the king of the Turks, Qaysar of the Romans, Kisra of the Persians; or it is not applied to him except when Himyar and Hadramawt are under him, as in the Qamus; or except when Himyar, Saba' and Hadramawt are under him, as al-Tibi mentioned; and those who fit this description are more than one, as is not hidden from one who knows the histories. As for what preceded about his demolishing Samarqand, 'Abd al-Malik mentioned the opposite and attributed its demolition to Shamar ibn Ifriqis ibn Abrahah, one of the Tababi'ah also, who was long before the aforementioned Tubba'. He said: Shamar went out towards Iraq, then headed intending China, and entered the city of al-Sughd, demolished it, and it was named Shamar Kand, that is, Shamar ruined it; then it was Arabized and became Samarqand. The account of the building can be attributed to this Shamar, for "kand" in the language of the people of Azerbaijan and its environs is said to mean "village," so Samarqand means "the village of Shamar," and this is more fitting to the building. Our contemporary scholar Mulla Amin Effendi al-'Umari al-Mawsili, may Allah cover him with His mercy, mentioned in his book Sharh Dhat al-Shifa' that the Tubba' mentioned earlier is Ibn Hassan, and that he ruled the whole world, and that he is called al-Ra'ish because he distributed gifts to people; perhaps what he said is the view of some, for Ibn Qutaybah said he is Ibn Kalikarb.

In the explanation of Ibn Abdun's qasida, it is stated that al-Ra'ish is a title of al-Harith ibn Badr, one of the Tababi'a (the Tubba' kings of Yemen). He lived a very long time before As'ad, mentioned earlier. He is also among those who mentioned our Prophet (ﷺ) in his poetry, when he said:

*And after them a great man will rule,*
*A prophet who does not permit what is forbidden.*
*He will be named Ahmad. Would that I*
*Might live a year after his emergence.*

Furthermore, his rule over the entire world is not accepted. In general, the reports about the Tubba' and their circumstances, and the order of their kings, are conflicting. Indeed, the author of *Tawarikh al-Umam* (Histories of the Nations) said: "There is no history more unreliable than the history of the kings of Himyar, because of the large number of years attributed to them alongside the small number of their kings. Their kings were twenty-six, and their period was two thousand and twenty years."

Others said: "Their period was three thousand, two hundred and eighty-two years. After them, the Abyssinians ruled Yemen." And Allah the Exalted knows best the reality of the matter. The point relied upon here is that the Tubba' mentioned is As'ad Abu Karib, that he was a believer in our Prophet (ﷺ), and that he was upon the religion of Ibrahim (peace be upon him), but he was not a prophet. The narration of his prophethood from Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him and his father) is not authentic. His foreknowledge of the Prophet's (ﷺ) mission does not imply prophethood, because he learned that from the rabbis of the Jews, who recognized it from the heavenly scriptures.

As for what is reported, that the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said: "I do not know whether Tubba' was a prophet or not," it is not established. However, Abu Dawud and al-Hakim reported that he (peace and blessings be upon him) said: "I do not know whether Dhu al-Qarnayn was [a prophet] or not." There is nothing in this that indicates hesitation about his prophethood or its absence, since Dhu al-Qarnayn is not a prophet according to the sound view. Moreover, it is apparent that the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) afterwards came to know that he was not Dhu al-Qarnayn.

Some said: the word Tubba' here does not refer to a single man, but rather to the kings of Yemen. This is contrary to the apparent meaning, and the reports refute it. The meaning of Tubba' is "one who is followed" (matbu'), so it is the pattern *fu'all* in the sense of *maf'ul*. This word may also come in the sense of *fa'il*, as it is said of the shadow that it is a *tubba'*, because it follows the sun. The kings of Yemen are called *aqyal*, from the phrase "so-and-so *yaqil* his father," meaning he follows his example, because they are followed. It was also said: their king was called *qil* because of the effectiveness of his words, and it is the lightened form of *qayyil*, like *mayyit*.

﴿And those before them﴾, that is, before the people of Tubba', such as ʿAd and Thamud, or before Quraysh. This is a generalization after a specification. ﴿We destroyed them﴾ is a new sentence explaining the outcome of their affair, by which He threatens the disbelievers of Quraysh. Or it is a circumstantial clause (*hal*), with *qad* implied or not, or from the pronoun hidden in the relative clause. Or it is the predicate of the relative pronoun, if the latter is taken as the subject and is not coordinated with what precedes it. ﴿Indeed they were criminals﴾ is a causal clause explaining their destruction, meaning: We destroyed them because of their being criminals. Therefore, let the disbelievers of Quraysh beware of destruction because of their own criminality.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 44, verse 38:

﴿And We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them﴾ i.e., what is between the two kinds (jinsayn), and this includes what is between the layers (tabaqat).

And ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr read (wa-mā baynahunna), so the pronoun refers to the collective of the heavens and the earth. ﴿In play﴾ i.e., in vain (ʿabithin), and this is evidence for the occurrence of the Resurrection (ḥashr), as has passed in al-Anbiya' and elsewhere.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 44, verse 39:

﴿We did not create them﴾ i.e., and what is between them, ﴿except with truth﴾. This is an exceptive clause (istithna' mufarragh, "emptied exception," in which the excluded element is left unstated) taken from the most general of states: i.e., We did not create them while being associated with anything, except while being associated with the truth. Thus the prepositional phrase (al-jar wa al-majrur) is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) relative to the subject (the agent, al-fa'il). It is also permitted that it be in the position of a circumstantial clause relative to the object (al-maf'ul), and the bi' (ba', "with") is for association (li al-mulabasah) in both of them. It is also permitted that it be causal (li al-sababiyyah), and the exception is then an emptied exception taken from the most general of causes: i.e., We did not create them by any cause among causes, except by the cause of the truth, which is faith, obedience, resurrection and recompense. The sense of association is the more apparent. ﴿But most of them do not know﴾. This is a concluding statement (tadhyil) and a severe rebuke of ignorance directed at those who deny the gathering (al-hashr), and an emphasis, because their denial leads to the nullification of all existent things entirely. ﴿And you reckon it to be trivial, while with God it is momentous﴾. For this reason the believers said: ﴿Our Lord, You did not create this in vain; glory be to You; so protect us from the punishment of the Fire﴾.

﴿Indeed, the Day of Decision﴾, meaning the separation of truth from falsehood and of the one who is right from the one who is wrong through recompense, or the separation of a person from his beloved ones and his relatives. ﴿Their appointed time﴾ is the time of their promise. ﴿All of them﴾. It is also read as (مِيقاتَهُمْ) with the accusative, in which case it is the subject of inna (the emphatic particle), and the predicate is (يَوْمُ الفَصْلِ), meaning: indeed the appointed time of their reckoning and their recompense is on the Day of Decision. It is not like inna ḥurrāsunā asadan (an example in which inna governs the noun in the accusative, and the sentence means "indeed our guards are lions").

﴿A day when no ally will avail﴾ is either a substitute (badal) for ﴿the Day of Decision﴾, or an explicative apposition ('atf bayan) according to those who do not require agreement (mutabaqah) in definiteness and indefiniteness. It was also permitted to put it in the accusative, with an implied verb "a'ni" (I mean). It may be a temporal adverb (zarf) governed by what is indicated by "al-fasl" (the decision), not by "al-fasl" itself, because a foreign element separates them. The verbal noun (masdar) does not govern when it is separated, because of its weakness. Or it may be governed by "al-fasl" itself, according to the view of one who tolerates separation when the object is an adverb, such as Ibn al-Hajib and al-Radi. Abu al-Baqa' permitted it to be an attribute (sifah) of "miqatuhum" (their appointed time). It was objected that it is indeclinable (jamid) and indefinite, because it is annexed (mudaf) to a clause, so how can it be an attribute of a definite noun? Moreover, according to the Basrans, its indeclinability is not valid when it is annexed to a clause whose beginning is inflected, and that is the present tense. That is, the meaning is "the day when a mawla will not avail..."

﴿a mawla [ally] will not avail a mawla [ally] anything﴾ of the sort of [enrichment/help], that is, in any manner of recompense. So "shay'an" (anything) is in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar), and it may also be the direct object. "Yughni" (avails) here means "yadfa'" (repels) and "yanfa'" (benefits). The indefiniteness of "shay'an" is for minimizing. The mawla is the companion who, by his nature, takes responsibility for assisting his companion in his affairs. This includes the paternal cousin (ibn al-'amm), the ally by oath (hilf), the freed slave ('atiq), the one who frees him (mu'tiq), and others. Al-Khafaji mentioned that it derives from al-wilayah, which is authority or disposal (tasarruf). So it includes everyone who exercises disposal over another for some matter, such as kinship or friendship. This is close to what we have mentioned. In any case, this is not the use of a homonym (mushtarak) in more than one meaning. Even if it were granted that there is a homonym used in more than one meaning, the verse would be evidence for Ibn al-Humam, may Allah have mercy on him, regarding the permissibility of that in negation. Thus, according to him, one says: "I did not see an eye (ayn)," meaning the eye of sight, the gold ('ayn al-dhahab, spring of gold) and others. And it is understood from the negation of a mawla's ability to avail that the negation of the ability of others to avail is included, a fortiori.

﴿nor will they be helped﴾. The pronoun, according to a group, refers to the first mawla, and the plural is by consideration of meaning, because it is an indefinite noun in the context of negation, and it generalizes. It does not refer to the second mawla, because that is more beneficial and more eloquent. This is because the state of the second mawla, that he is not helped, is known from the earlier negation of availing. Also, if he does not help the one who relies on him, how then could he himself be helped? Also, the reason for the plural pronoun is more apparent here. It was permitted that it refers to the second, to indicate that he is not helped by anyone other than his mawla, and this is also in the context of negation, although it does not reach the rank of the first in that. Yes, it has been said regarding the reason for the plural referring to both: an indefinite noun in the context of negation indicates every single individual, so the pronoun does not return to it in the plural. It was answered that this is not a consistent rule, because it may be treated as a collective, by the indication of the plural pronoun returning to it. Perhaps the better view is that the pronoun returns to the mawla understood from the negated indefinite noun. Some said: If the pronoun were made to refer to the disbelievers, like the pronoun in "miqatuhum" (their appointed time), the benefit would be increased and the effort lessened. So reflect.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 44, verse 42:

﴿Except him on whom Allah has mercy.﴾ It is in a position of raising (marfu') as a substitute (badal) for the pronoun in (yunsarun, "they are helped"), or in a position of nasb as an exception (istithna') from it. That is: none is prevented from the punishment except the one whom Allah, exalted is He, has mercy upon, and that is by pardoning him and accepting intercession for him.

It is also permitted that it be a substitute or an exception from (mawla, "a protector/friend"). In this, as in the first, there is evidence for the establishment of intercession. However, the preference lies with the first, both in wording and in meaning. The exception from whichever it is is connected (muttasil). Al-Kisa'i (al-Kisa'i) said that it is disconnected (munqati'), meaning: "but whomever Allah, exalted is He, has mercy upon," for he has no need of a relative to benefit him nor of a helper to aid him. There is no basis for this when the connection is evident. Yes, it is not possible on the reading that the exception is from the pronoun and that it refers to the disbelievers, so take note.

﴿Indeed, He is the Mighty⌃, the Merciful⌃﴾: the Mighty (al-'Aziz) is the Overpowering, whom none can help against one whom He, glorified is He, wills to punish; the Merciful (al-Rahim) is to whomever He, mighty and majestic, wills to show mercy.

[p. 133]

﴿Indeed, the tree of zaqqum﴾: the meaning of zaqqum has already been explained in Surat al-Saffat. It is also read as ﴿shajarata﴾ with a kasra on the shin. ﴿The food of the sinner﴾: that is, the one who commits many sins. Here the intended meaning is the disbeliever, because of what comes before and after it, which points to this meaning and not to a general sense that would include the disobedient person who commits many sins. Moreover, the intended meaning is the category of disbeliever, not one specific individual. Ibn Zayd and Sa'id ibn Jubayr said that the sinner here is Abu Jahl. This is not valid, and there is no evidence for it, except what Sa'id ibn Mansur reported from Abu Malik: that Abu Jahl used to bring dates and butter and say, "Eat zaqqum, for this is the zaqqum that Muhammad (ﷺ) promises you," and then ﴿Indeed, the tree of zaqqum, the food of the sinner﴾ was revealed. This is so for reasons that are not hidden. A similar report says that the sinner is al-Walid. Abu 'Ubayd in his Fada'il and Ibn al-Anbari and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Awf ibn 'Abd Allah that Ibn Mas'ud taught a man ﴿Indeed, the tree of zaqqum, the food of the sinner﴾, and the man said, "the food of the orphan (yatim)." He repeated it to him, but his tongue would not produce it correctly. So he said, "Can you say 'the food of the wicked (fajir)'?" He said, "Yes." He said, "Then do so." Al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and a group reported from Abu al-Darda' that the same thing happened to him. When he saw that the man did not understand, he said, "Indeed, the tree of zaqqum is the food of the wicked."

From this it has been inferred that replacing one word with another in place of it is permissible if the replacement conveys the same meaning. Al-Qadi Abu Bakr in al-Intisar objected to this, saying that Ibn Mas'ud intended to alert him that he did not mean the orphan but the wicked, so he should recite "al-athim." You know that this interpretation hardly applies to what is reported from Ibn Mas'ud, for it is almost explicit in permitting the substitution for that man. Even further from this interpretation is what Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ubayy, that he used to teach a Persian man, and whenever he recited to him ﴿Indeed, the tree of zaqqum, the food of the sinner﴾, the man would say, "the food of the orphan." The Prophet (ﷺ) passed by him and said, "Tell him: the food of the dark-skinned (zallam)." He said it, and his tongue became fluent with it. There are many reports on this matter with sound chains, such as the report of Ahmad from Abu Hurayra: "The Qur'an was revealed in seven ahruf, [ending with] 'ʿAlīman ḥakīman ghafūran raḥīman'." And like his report from Abu Bakra: "All of it," that is, the Qur'an, "is healing and sufficient, so long as you do not end a verse of punishment with mercy, or a verse of mercy with punishment, such as saying 'come, approach, hurry, hasten,' and the like." However, al-Tahawi said: this was only a concession when it was difficult for many of them to recite with one fixed wording, because they did not know writing, precise preservation, and mastery of memorization. Then it was abrogated (naskh) when the excuse ended and writing and memorization became easy. Ibn 'Abd al-Barr, al-Baqillani, and others said the same. Perhaps, if a substitution by one of the Companions after him (peace be upon him) is established, it is said that it occurred before they learned of the abrogation. When the substitution of one word for another that conveys the same meaning is not permitted, even within the same Arabic language, then the impermissibility of doing so across differing languages, such as Arabic and Persian, is more evident. As for what is reported from Imam Abu Hanifa (may Allah be pleased with him), that he considered it permissible to recite the Qur'an in Persian provided the meanings are conveyed in full, it is established from him that the opposite is true. Al-Shurunbulali (may Allah have mercy on him) examined this question in a separate treatise with unmatched thoroughness, and something of this has already been mentioned in this book, so recall it.

"Al-ta'am" is what is eaten of food. Its origin is a verbal noun (masdar), and for this reason it occurs as a predicate referring to a feminine subject without agreement. It has also been permitted that this is of the type of the poet's saying:

"The illumination of reason is eclipsed by obedience to desire, while the reason of one who disobeys desire grows in illumination."

Thus it is as if it were said: "Indeed, zaqqum is the food of the sinner."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 44, verse 45:

﴿Like molten brass (al-muhl)﴾ — the dregs of olive oil (ʿakar al-zayt), as related from Ibn ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with them both. And in a ḥadīth narrated by al-Ḥākim and others from Abu Saʿid, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), it is said: "When it is brought near to his face — meaning the one of Hell — the skin of his face will fall off." It may be supported by His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿On the Day when the sky will be like molten brass (al-muhl)﴾, together with His saying: ﴿And it will become rose-red like oil (al-dihān)﴾. Some said: the dregs of tar (ʿakar al-qaṭirān). In a narration from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, it is "pus" (al-ṣadīd). From the same usage is what is in the ḥadīth of Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him: "Bury me in these two garments of mine, for they are only for al-muhl and the dust." And in another narration from him, may Allah be pleased with him, that whatever is melted of gold, silver, iron or lead [is called muhl]. The same is related from Ibn Masʿud. It was said: it is called muhl because it is left (yumhal) in the fire until it melts, so it is from al-mahal, in the sense of stillness (al-sukūn). Some claimed it is a homonym (al-ishtirāk), and its usage has come for everything you have heard. Al-Ḥasan read (kal-mahl) with a fatḥa on the mīm, and it is a dialectal form of it. The prepositional phrase (al-jārr wa-l-majrūr), or the kāf, is in the place of raf' as the predicate of an omitted subject (mubtada'), and the sentence is a resumptive statement (istiʾnāf) explaining the condition of the food, i.e., it is like al-muhl or the like of al-muhl. His saying, mighty and majestic is He, ﴿boiling in the bellies﴾, is a second predicate of that subject. It was said: it is a ḥāl (circumstantial clause) from the pronoun hidden in the prepositional phrase, so it is also a description of the food. Abu ʿUbayd said: it is a ḥāl from al-muhl. It was said: it is a ṣifa (qualifier) of it, because the alif-lam in it is for the genus, like the verse:

"I pass by the miser who insults me"

and it is considered included in the comparison. You know that the boiling of food in the belly contains exaggeration, but the comparison with muhl boiling in the belly is not. It was said: kal-muhl or the kāf is a second predicate of inna, and the sentence ﴿boiling in the bellies﴾ is a ḥāl from the zaqqūm or the food. It was objected that the coming of a ḥāl from a mudāf ilayhi is prohibited except in specific forms, and this is not one of them, and that it is prohibited to come from the predicate and from the subject. It was answered that this is based on the permissibility of a ḥāl coming from the predicate and from the subject, and that the mudāf ilayhi which is the subject is in its ruling, and that the forms mentioned in which a ḥāl comes from the mudāf ilayhi are because the mudāf is like a part in permissibility of its omission. It is not hidden that this is built on a weak opinion. It was said: kal-muhl is a second predicate and the sentence is a ḥāl from the hidden pronoun of the tree in it, and the masculine form is due to considering it as the food of the sinner, or because of its acquiring that to which it is attributed, similar to what you heard in the verse just above; and this is an artificial position that is dispensable. It was said: the sentence in that case is the predicate of an omitted subject which is the pronoun of the food or the zaqqūm; if the sentence is then resumptive, the matter is easy, but if it is a ḥāl, the earlier problem returns, and I do not think you consider it easy. It was said: kal-muhl is a ḥāl from ṭaʿām (food), and its ḥāl is known. In sum, the aspects of the i'rab of the verse are many, and I choose from them what I mentioned first.

ʿAmr ibn Maymūn, Abu Razīn, al-Aʿraj, Abu Jaʿfar, Shayba, Ibn Muḥaysin, Ṭalḥa, and al-Ḥasan in one narration, and most of the Seven read (taghlī) with a feminine ta' (tāʾ fawqiyya). Then kal-muhl is a second predicate of inna, and the sentence (taghlī) is a third predicate. The unity of the subject and predicate ensures the unity of the two readings in meaning, so understand this and do not be negligent.

ِ﴿Like the boiling of scalding water﴾. It is an attributive adjective of a deleted verbal noun (maṣdar), meaning: a boiling like the boiling of scalding water (al-ḥamīm). It is also permitted that it be a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl). Al-ḥamīm is that which is at the utmost degree of heat.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 44, verse 47:

﴿Seize him⦆ according to the implied speech, the one addressed being the zabaniyah (the angels of punishment), i.e., "It will be said to them: Seize him." ﴿Then drag him⦆ forcibly.

Al-Raghib said: al-'atl (seizing) is taking hold of a thing by its middle and dragging it by force. Some express it with "garment" instead of "thing," but that is not necessary; the essential point is dragging together with seizing firmly and roughly.

Al-A'mash and Mujahid said: the meaning of (i'tilawhu) is "break him," as firewood is broken. The apparent reading of this requires either an implied element (tadmin) or attaching the prepositional phrase to the verb (khadhwuhu). The first meaning is the well-known one. Zayd ibn 'Ali, the two Hijazis, Ibn 'Amir and Ya'qub read (fa'tulluhu) with a damma on the ta', and this is reported from al-Hasan, Qatadah and al-A'raj, on the basis that it is from the pattern of qa'ada. The reading of the majority is from the pattern of nasara, and both are dialectal forms (lughatan). ﴿Into the midst of the Blazing Fire⦆: i.e., its center. It is called sawa' (midst) because the distance of all its sides from it is equal.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 44, verse 48:

﴿Then pour over his head some of the torment of the boiling water.﴾ It is as if its original form was: "Pour over his head the boiling water (al-hamim)," and then it was said: "Pour over his head a torment which is the boiling water," for emphasis (mubalaghah), by making the torment identical with the boiling water. This is consequent upon it, and by making it something poured like a perceptible thing. Then the torment was attributed to the boiling water (idafah) for lightness (al-takhfif), and "min" (some of) was added to indicate that what is poured is a part of this kind. So here there is either a simile (tamthil), or a clear metaphor (isti'arah tasrihiyyah), or an implied metaphor (isti'arah makniyyah), or an imaginative metaphor (isti'arah takhyiliyyah).

Al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 44, verse 49:

﴿Taste it! Indeed, you are the mighty, the noble.﴾ Meaning: it may be said, or they may be told to say to him, this as mockery and rebuke for what he used to claim.

Abd al-Razzaq and others related from Qatada, who said: When ﴿Seize him and drag him into the midst of the Blazing Fire﴾ was revealed, Abu Jahl said: "Between its two mountains (Mecca's), there is no man more mighty or more noble than I." So Allah the Exalted said: "Taste it," and so on.

Al-Umawi, in his Maghazi, related from Ikrima that Abu Jahl said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Neither you nor your companion can do anything for me. You know that I am the most protected of the people of al-Batha (the valley of Mecca), and I am the mighty, the noble." Then Allah the Exalted killed him on the day of Badr, humiliated him, and reproached him with his words: ﴿Taste it! Indeed, you are the mighty, the noble.﴾

It is also related that the accursed one said one day: "O assembly of Quraysh, tell me what my name is." Three names were mentioned to him: Amr, al-Jallas, and Abu al-Hakam. He said: "You have not hit my name. Shall I not tell you it?" They said: "Yes." He said: "My name is al-Aziz al-Karim (the mighty, the noble)." Then there was revealed ﴿Indeed, the tree of zaqqum...﴾ and the verses that follow.

This and similar reports also do not indicate that the ruling of the verse is restricted to him. Every sinner who makes such a claim will be told the same on the Day of Resurrection. It has also been said that the meaning is: "Taste it! Indeed, you were mighty among your people and noble in their eyes," but that did not benefit you or avail you anything. The word al-dhawq (tasting) is used metaphorically for perception.

Al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with them both) recited it from the pulpit, and al-Kisa'i read ﴿أنَّكَ﴾ (annaka) with a fatha on the hamza, meaning "because you are" (li-annaka).

Indeed, this (﴿إنَّ هَذا﴾) — that is, the punishment, or the matter in which you are — ﴿is what you used to doubt﴾ (﴿ما كُنْتُمْ بِهِ تَمْتَرُونَ﴾): you were in doubt about it and disputed concerning it. This is the beginning of a speech from Him, mighty and majestic, or it is part of what is being said (maqul al-qawl). The plural is used in consideration of the meaning, as you have heard, that the intended referent is the category of the sinner (jins al-athim).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 44, verses 51–52:

﴿Indeed, the God-fearing will be in a station﴾ — in a place of standing. By "standing" is meant steadfastness and constant abiding, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿except while you stand over him [constantly]﴾. It is used as a metaphor for residence, since one who resides remains constantly in his place; and this is what is meant by those who said: "in a station," that is, a place of residence.

ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with them both, Zayd ibn ʿAli, Abu Jaʿfar, Shayba, al-Aʿraj, al-Hasan, Qatada, Nafi, and Ibn ʿAmir recited (muqam) with a dammah on the mim, and its meaning is "a place of residence." According to what we have established, both readings return to one meaning.

﴿Secure﴾ — whose companion feels safe from what he dislikes. It is thus an adjective derived from security (amn), which is the absence of fear regarding what is of concern to him. Describing the station as such is based on the security of those who believe in it, so it is a metaphorical attribution (isnad majazi), as in "a flowing river." The apparent sense of al-Zamakhshari's words is that this is a metaphor drawn from trust (amanah), as if the place were a trusted deposit in whose keeping are placed things that protect its occupants from hardships. Hence there is a implicit and imaginative metaphor (istiʿarah makniyyah wa takhyiliyyah). Ibn ʿAtiyya said: "faʿil" here means "maf ul," that is, "one in whom there is security," but this is not correct. It is also permitted that it denotes attribution, that is, "possessing security."

﴿In gardens and springs﴾ — a substitution (badal) for (station), with the preposition repeated, or the prepositional phrase is a substitution for the prepositional phrase. The locative sense of "springs" is by contiguity (mujawarah). The apparent view is that it is a substitution of inclusion (badal ishtimal), not of whole for part. In this is an indication of the purity of their place and its containing what is pleasant of foods and drinks.

﴿They will wear [garments] of sundus and istabraq﴾ is either a second predicate (khabar thani), or a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of the pronoun in the preposition-and-object phrase, or a resumed sentence (isti'naf).

Tha'lab said: sundus (سُنْدُس) is the fine part of dibaj (brocade silk), and its singular is sundusa (سُنْدُسَة). Istabraq (إسْتَبْرَق) is its thick part. Al-Layth said: it is a kind of buzyun (a heavy cloth), made from al-mar'az (a soft, fine wool). Some scholars have said that the lexicographers did not disagree that both words are Arabicised (mu'arrab, borrowed from another language and adapted to Arabic).

In al-Kashshaf: istabraq is the thick part of dibaj, and it is an Arabicisation of istabar (اِسْتَبَر). Al-Khafaji said: the meaning of istabar in the Persian language is "thick" in general, and then it was specialised to thick dibaj and Arabicised. It has also been said that it is an Arabic word derived from al-baraqa (glitter), and this was supported by reading it with a connected hamza (wasl al-hamza). This, as you see, is weak.

Some scholars mentioned that sundus originally is sindi (سِنْدِيّ), meaning "related to al-Sind," the well-known region, because sundus used to be imported from there. The ya' of relation (ya' al-nisba) was changed to sin (س). The discussion of this has already passed, so recall it. Furthermore, the occurrence of an Arabicised word in the Great Qur'an does not contradict its being a clear Arabic text.

The author of al-Kashf quoted Jar Allah (al-Zamakhshari) as saying: the composed speech is made of letters that are spread out in any language, whether Turkish, Persian or Arabic, and this does not indicate that Arabic is non-Arabic; so it is the same here. Then the author of al-Kashf said: he means that the fact that istabar is non-Arabic does not necessarily mean that istabraq is the same.

Ibn Muhaysin read (وَاسْتَبْرَقَ) as a past-tense verb, as in al-Bahr. In that case, the clause is said to be parenthetical (mu'tarida), and it is also said to be a circumstantial qualifier of (sundus). The meaning is: they wear sundus while it has shone (بَرَقَ) because of its polish and its great beauty.

﴿reclining face to face﴾ in their assemblies, so that each of them may enjoy the company of the other.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 44, verse 54:

﴿Thus﴾, that is, the matter is thus. The *kaf* (the particle "like") here is in the nominative position as a predicate to a deleted subject, and the purpose is to affirm and confirm what has passed.

It is related from Jar Allah (al-Zamakhshari) that he said: "Its meaning is that the description does not fully encompass it, and that it is like something which no description can encompass. So it is as if it were said: the matter is like that and what resembles it."

What the meticulous scholar (al-Muddaqqiq) intended is that the *kaf* is superfluous (*muqhan*), for emphasis (*mubalaghah*), and this is consistent in the usage of both the Arabs and non-Arabs (*al-'Ajam*). It has also been allowed that it is in the accusative position, in the sense of "We gave them the like of that," and the words of the Exalted, ﴿and We married them﴾, are on this reading a conjunction to the deleted verb, and to what precedes it, "they wear" (*yalbasun*). The purpose, according to what many have said, is ﴿and We paired them with Hur 'In﴾. It has been interpreted this way, it is said, because there is no obligation in Paradise, so there is no contract (*'aqd*) and no marriage in the commonly understood sense. It is also said that it is because of the preposition (*ba'*), and that *zawwajahu al-mar'ah* in the sense of *ankahahu iyyaha* is transitive by itself. In this there is a discussion, for al-Akhfash permitted the *ba'* with it, so one says *zawwajtuhu bi-imra'ah* and he married her; and the tribe of Azd Shanu'ah also construe it with *ba'*. In the *Qamus* it is stated: "*Zawwajtuhu imra'ah* and *tazawwajtu imra'ah*, and *bi-ha* or *hiya*," which is rare. From what has been mentioned, it is known that the statement of some jurists, "I married him to her" (*zawwajtuhu biha*), is an error with no justification. It may be said that this interpretation is acceptable, because the Hur 'In in Paradise are property of the right hand (*milk yamin*), like concubines (*sarari*) in this world, so the matter does not require a contract over them. Moreover, it is possible that there is a contract in Paradise even though there is no obligation in it.

Ibn Jarir and others have related from Mujahid that he said: "*Zawwajnahum*: we gave them in marriage (*ankahnahum*)." Some people have said there is obligation in Paradise in the sense of command and prohibition, but they find no burden in doing or abstaining. However, the well-known view is that there is no obligation in it. Some of what was forbidden in this world, such as marrying another's wife or marrying close relatives (*mahram*), they do not do, because it never occurs to their minds at all.

*Al-Hur* is the plural of *hawra'*, which means white, as related from Ibn 'Abbas, al-Dahhak and others. It has been said that it means one whose eye has intense blackness and whiteness. It has also been said that *al-hawra'* is one possessing *hawar*, which is the blackness of the whole pupil, as in gazelles, and so it is only used of humans metaphorically. Ibn al-Mundhir and others have related from Mujahid that *al-hawra'* is one in whom the gaze is bewildered (*yahar fiha al-tarf*). *Al-'In* is the plural of *'ayna'*, which means one with large eyes. Most reports indicate that they are
[p. 136]
not the women of this world. Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Tabarani have related from Abu Umamah, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'The Hur 'In were created from saffron.'" Ibn Mardawayh and al-Khatib have related from Anas ibn Malik, as a marfu' report, something similar.

Ibn al-Mubarak has related from Zayd ibn Aslam who said: "Indeed Allah the Exalted did not create the Hur 'In from dust; He created them only from musk, camphor and saffron."

Ibn Mardawayh and al-Daylami have related from 'A'ishah, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'The Hur 'In were created from the glorification (*tasbih*) of the angels, peace be upon them.'" If this is authentic, it does not contradict what came before it, for it must be said that meanings take on bodily form (*tajassud al-ma'ani*), so it is permissible for glorification to take on form and to be made a part of that from which they were created. It has also been said that what is meant by them here is the women of this world, who in Paradise are Hur 'In in the sense you have heard. Indeed they are more beautiful than the Hur 'In, I mean the women created in Paradise from saffron or otherwise. A man there is given the wives he had in this world, and to that may be added whomever Allah the Exalted wills of women who died and did not marry. As for a woman who married more than one husband, she belongs to her last husband, or to her first if he did not divorce her in this world, or she is given a choice and chooses whichever of them was best in character toward her. These are opinions, and a group among them has declared the first to be sound. The wife of an unbeliever who entered Paradise is given to whomever Allah the Exalted wills. It has been reported that Asiyah, the wife of Pharaoh, will be the wife of our Prophet (ﷺ).

'Ikrimah read *bi-hur 'in* with the genitive construction (*idafah*), and it is in the sense of *min*, that is, "with the Hur from the 'In." In the reading of 'Abd Allah it is *bi-'Is 'In*, and *al-'Aysa'* is white with a reddish tinge overlying it.

They call therein for every kind of fruit, seeking and ordering the bringing of whatever fruits they desire, and no particular fruit is restricted to a place or a time. ﴿Secure﴾ from harm of any kind whatsoever. This is a circumstantial clause (hal) referring to the subject pronoun in ﴿they call﴾. That it be a circumstantial clause relating to the pronoun in His words, glorified is He, ﴿in gardens﴾, is far-fetched, and even further from this is making ﴿yad'una﴾ (they call) in that case a qualifying attribute (sifah) of the ḥūr (companions with beautiful eyes), with the nūn in it being the pronoun of the feminine plural, its pattern being yaf'alna, because of what it involves of departing from the apparent meaning (khilaf al-zahir) together with its lack of fit with the context (al-munasabah li-l-siyaq).

The Qur'anic phrase ﴿They do not taste therein death, except the first death﴾ is either a resumptive clause (jumlah musta'nafah) or a circumstantial clause (jumlah haliyyah). It is as if it were meant to be said: "They do not taste death therein at all," but He placed "the first death" in place of that, because the death that has already passed cannot be tasted in the future. This is therefore of the type of conditioning on the impossible (al-ta'liq bil-muhal), as if it were said: "If the first death can be tasted in the future, then they will taste it." A parallel to this is the saying of one who is asked for water by someone: "I will not give you to drink except the embers," though it is known that embers are not drunk. Similarly is the statement of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And do not marry those whom your fathers married of women, except what has already passed﴾. Thus the exception is connected (istithna' muttasil), and the entry [into Paradise] is an assumed supposition (dukhul far'i) for the sake of emphasis. The pronoun in "therein" (fiha) refers to the Gardens. It has been said that the exception is connected and that the believer, at the time of his death, witnesses what he will be given in Paradise, so it is as if he were therein, and thus he has tasted the first death in Paradise. It has also been said that the exception is connected and the pronoun "therein" refers to the Hereafter, and death is the first of its states; the difficulty in this, together with the commission of figurative usage, is not hidden. It has also been said that the exception is disjunctive (istithna' munqati') and the pronoun refers to the Gardens, meaning: "But the first death, they have indeed tasted it in this world." The original principle is the connection of the exception.

Al-Tabari said: "Illa" here means "after" (ba'da). The majority of scholars did not accept this meaning for it. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "A group of people held that 'illa' means 'other than' (siwa), and al-Tabari declared this weak."

Abu Hayyan said: "His weakening of it is not correct; rather the meaning is sound with the sense of 'other than' (siwa) and it is coherent."

The benefit of the description is to remind of the state of this world.

The reason for all the aspects you have heard is to answer an objection raised here: that the first death is among what has passed for them in this world, and what is of this nature cannot be tasted in Paradise, so how can it be made an exception? It has been said that the objection is based on the premise that an exception from a negation is an affirmation, so the excluded (mustathna) takes on the ruling negated from the excluded-from (mustathna minhu), and it is impossible that the past first death should be attributed the tasting in Paradise. As for the view of the one who took it as a speech that continues after a pause (takallum bil-baqi ba'da al-thunya), meaning: "They do not taste other than the first death from death," there is then no difficulty, so reflect.

'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr read ﴿لا يُذاقُونَ﴾ in the passive voice. 'Abd Allah (Ibn Mas'ud) read ﴿They do not taste therein the taste of death﴾.

A hadith has come: "Sleep is the brother of death." It was narrated by al-Bazzar, al-Tabarani in al-Awsat, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th with a sound chain (bi-sanad sahih), from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, who said: "It was said: 'O Messenger of God, do the people of Paradise sleep?' He said: 'No. Sleep is the brother of death, and the people of Paradise do not die and do not sleep.'" (ﷺ)

And He saved them from the punishment of the Blazing Fire. Abu Haywa recited (wa-waqqahum), with the qaf doubled, for the sake of intensifying the magnitude of the protection (muballagha fi al-takthir fi al-wiqaya), because the tafʻil form here serves to increase the meaning and not to make the verb transitive, since the verb is already transitive before it. ﴿As a bounty from your Lord⦆ meaning: they were given all of that as a gift and an act of grace from Him, exalted is He; so it is in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar). It is also permitted that it be a circumstantial accusative (hal) or an accusative of purpose (maf'ul lahu). In any case, there is in it an indication of the negation of their deeds obligating reward from Him, glorified and exalted is He. It was also read as (fadlun) in the nominative, meaning: that is a bounty. ﴿That is indeed the great triumph⦆ because it is a triumph in attaining what is sought and a deliverance from what is hateful.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 44, verse 58:

﴿So indeed We have made it easy﴾, that is, indeed We have made the Qur'an easy ﴿in your tongue﴾, that is, in your language. It was also said: the meaning is that We sent it down upon your tongue without writing, because he was unlettered (ummi). This is a summary and a compendium (fadhlakah) of what is in the surah after detail, a reminder of what has preceded explained within it. So the meaning is: remind them with the Clear Book, for indeed We have made it easy in your tongue. ﴿So that they may remember﴾, that is, so that they may understand it, be reminded by it, and act in accordance with its requirements.

﴿So wait﴾, that is: even if they do not take heed, wait for what will befall them. This is a generalization after a specification made by His words, ﴿So watch for the day when the sky will bring forth a visible smoke﴾ (44:10), and so on. ﴿Indeed they too are waiting﴾, meaning they are waiting for what will befall you, as they said, ﴿We await for him the misfortunes of time﴾ (52:30). It has also been said that its meaning is "they are awaited" (muraqqabun), i.e., they are waiting for what will befall them, by way of mockery (tahakkum). It has also been said that it is an instance of musha-kalah (a figure in which a word is used because of its association with a nearby word), and the meaning is that they are destined for punishment. In the verse there is a promise to him (ﷺ) that is not hidden. It has also been said that the verse contains a command to disengage (from them), and that this is abrogated (mansukh) by the verse of the sword (ayat al-sayf), so do not be heedless.

Among the allusive (ishari) readings of the verses is what they mention concerning His words, ﴿And We had already tested before them the people of Pharaoh﴾ (44:17), through to the end of the story, namely applying this to what is within the souls (al-anfus). This is known from what we have mentioned in the chapter on allusion (bab al-ishara) in this book more than once, so we will not lengthen on it.

They also said concerning His words, ﴿And We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them in play﴾ (44:38), ﴿We did not create them except with truth﴾ (44:39), that it is an allusion to Unity, like His words, ﴿We will show them Our signs in the horizons and within themselves until it becomes clear to them that it is the Truth﴾ (41:53). Some of them stated it more plainly and said: the Truth is He, Mighty and Majestic, and the "ba" (in bi-l-haqq) is causal, meaning: We did not create them except because of the cause that they be mirrors for the manifestation of the Truth, exalted is He. As for those among them who took the "ba" to indicate accompaniment (mulabasah), they recited:

The glass grew fine and the wine grew clear, so they became alike, and the matter became confused.
So it is as if there is wine but no cup, and as if there is a cup but no wine.

The expression is narrow, the matter lies beyond the reach of the intellect, and silence is safer.

They also said concerning the tree of zaqqum (44:43–44), that it is the tree of greed and love of this world, which will appear on the Day of Resurrection in the worst condition and the most foul taste. And they said that ﴿the first death﴾ (44:56) is what occurred in this world through killing the self with the sword of sincerity in the greatest jihad, and this is what is pointed to by "Die before you die." Whoever dies that death lives forever the good life, which nothing of the pain of the body or the spirit mixes with. That is ﴿the great triumph﴾. And Allah, the Exalted, says the truth, and He, glory be to Him, guides to the way.
